Al-Asamm said: The signs of Moses, peace be upon him, were: the staff, the hand, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the splitting of the sea, the gushing of springs from the rock, the shading of the mountain, and the sending down of manna and quails. Al-Jubba'i said: Allah sent Moses, peace be upon him, to his people, the Children of Israel, with His signs, which are His proofs and the Books revealed to him, and commanded him to make the religion clear to them. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: Allah, the Exalted, said in describing Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, that you might bring mankind out of darknesses into the light﴾, and said regarding Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿Bring your people out of darknesses into the light﴾. The purpose is to show that the aim of the mission is one and the same with respect to all the prophets, peace be upon them, namely, to strive to bring creation out of the darknesses of misguidance into the lights of guidance.

The second issue: al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿Bring your people out﴾ means: [it is] that you bring out your people. Then he said: ﴿An (that)﴾ here may be an explanatory particle meaning "i.e." (ay), and the meaning would be: "And We had already sent Moses with Our signs, i.e., bring out your people," as if the meaning were: "We said to him: Bring out your people." A similar usage is His saying: ﴿And the chiefs among them went forth, [saying]: "Walk on (an ni'mshū)"﴾ [Sad: 6], i.e., "Walk on," and the interpretation is: "It was said to them: Walk on." It may also be the light (mukhaffafa) an that is used for the report, and the meaning would be: "We sent him so that he would bring out his people," except that the preposition was omitted and "an" was joined to a verb in the imperative. A parallel is your saying: "I wrote to him that stand up (an qum)" and "I commanded him that stand up (an qum)." Then al-Zajjaj related these two opinions from Sibawayh.

As for His saying: ﴿And remind them of the Days of Allah﴾, know that Allah commanded Moses, peace be upon him, in this context with two things:

One of them: that he bring them out of the darknesses of disbelief.

The second: that he remind them of the Days of Allah. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: al-Wahidi said: "Ayyam (days)" is the plural of "yawm (day)," and the yawm is the measure of the period from the rising of the sun to its setting. The original form of "ayyam" was "ayway'm"; the waw and the ya' came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so one was assimilated into the other and the ya' prevailed.

The second issue: "Days" is used to refer to the great events that occurred in them. One says: "So-and-so is knowledgeable of the Days of the Arabs," meaning their battles. And in the proverb: "Whoever sees a day, a day will be seen by him"; its meaning is: whoever was seen on a day rejoicing at the downfall of another will be seen on another day sorrowful at his own downfall. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those days We alternate among the people﴾ [Al-i-Imran: 140].

Knowing this, the meaning is: admonish them with encouragement and warning, with promise and threat. Encouragement and promise is to remind them of what Allah bestowed upon them and upon those before them who believed in the messengers in all the days that passed; and warning and threat is to remind them of the might, punishment and retribution of Allah against those of the earlier nations who denied the messengers in the days that passed, like what befell 'Ad, Thamud and others of torment, so that they would be eager for the promise and believe, and beware of the threat and abandon denial.

Know that among the Days of Allah regarding Moses, peace be upon him, some were days of trial and affliction, namely the days in which the Children of Israel were under the oppression of Pharaoh, and some were days of ease and blessing, such as the sending down of manna and quails, the splitting of the sea, and the shading by the cloud.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one﴾. The meaning is that in that reminder and admonition are proofs for whoever is steadfast and grateful; because the state is either a state of affliction and calamity or a state of gift and bounty. If it is the first, the believer is steadfast; if it is the second, he is grateful. This is an indication that the believer must not let his time be free of one of these two matters: if the time passes in accordance with what suits his nature and agrees with his will, he is occupied with gratitude; and if it passes in what does not suit his nature, he is occupied with patience.

If it is said: These reminders are signs for all, so why did He single out the steadfast and grateful with them?

We say: There are several answers:

The first: since they were the ones who benefited from these signs, they became as if they were signs only for them, as in His saying: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] and His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45].

The second: it is not far-fetched to say that benefiting from this kind of reminder cannot be achieved except by one who is patient or grateful. As for one who is not such, he does not benefit from these signs.

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, mentioned that He commanded Moses, peace be upon him, to remind them of the Days of Allah, the Exalted, He related that Moses, peace be upon him, reminded them of them, saying: ﴿And when Moses said to his people: "Remember the favour of Allah upon you when He saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment"﴾. Here, His saying ﴿when He saved you﴾ is a time-adverb (zarf) for "favour," in the sense of "bounty," meaning: "Remember Allah's bounty upon you at that time."

* * *

Remaining in the verse are questions:

The first question: In Surat al-Baqarah it is mentioned: ﴿yudhabbihūna (slaughter)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 49] and in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿yuqattilūna (kill)﴾ [al-A'raf: 141], and here it is ﴿wa-yudhabbihūna (and slaughter)﴾ with the waw. What is the difference?

The answer: Allah, the Exalted, said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿yudhabbihūna﴾ without a waw, because it is an explanation of His saying: ﴿the worst torment﴾, and in explanation it is not good to mention the waw. You say: "The people came to me, Zayd and 'Amr," because you intended to explain "the people" by these two. Similarly His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ ﴿the punishment will be doubled for him﴾ [al-Furqan: 68-69]. Since "penalty (athām)" became explained by "doubling of the punishment," the waw was rightly omitted from it. In this surah, however, He introduced the waw, because the meaning is that they tormented them by means other than slaughter and also by slaughter; so His saying ﴿wa-yudhabbihūna (and slaughter)﴾ is another kind of torment, not an explanation of what precedes it.

The second question: How was the action of Pharaoh's people a trial from their Lord?

The answer is in two respects:

One of them: that Allah's granting them power until they did what they did was a trial from Allah.

The second, which is that this refers to the deliverance, and it is a great trial. Trial (balā') is testing (ibtila'), and that may sometimes be by blessing and at other times by affliction. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35]. This second view is preferable, because it agrees with the beginning of the verse, which is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when Moses said to his people: "Remember the favour of Allah upon you"﴾.

The third question: Suppose the slaughtering of the sons was a trial; how is the sparing of the women a trial?

The answer: They used them in service, sparing them as a favour in the sense of deliverance from death; and also, leaving them alone apart from men contains the greatest harms.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verse 7:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed, "If you are grateful, I will surely increase you; but if you are ungrateful, indeed My punishment is severe."﴾

Know that His saying ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed﴾ is part of what Musa (Moses) said to his people, as if it were said: "And when Musa said to his people: Remember the favour of Allah upon you, and remember when your Lord proclaimed..." The meaning of ﴿proclaimed﴾ (ta'adhdhana) is "your Lord announced" (adhina rabbukum). The counterpart of ta'adhdhana is ādhana, as with ta'awwada and awʿada (to threaten), and tafaḍḍala and afḍala (to bestow favour). In the pattern tafaʿʿala (the form with the doubled middle letter) there must be an added meaning not present in af'ala. It is as if it were said: "And when your Lord made a proclamation, an emphatic proclamation by which doubts are dispelled and suspicion is removed." The meaning is: "And when your Lord proclaimed." Then He said: ﴿If you are grateful﴾. Thus ta'adhdhana is treated as qāla (said), because it is a kind of speech. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): "And when your Lord said, 'If you are grateful...'"

Know also that the purpose of the verse is to show that whoever occupies himself with thanking the blessings of Allah, Allah increases him in His blessings. Here it is necessary to know the reality of gratitude and to inquire about those increased blessings that result from occupying oneself with gratitude. As for gratitude, it is an expression of acknowledging the benefactor's favour together with glorifying him and settling the soul upon this course. As for the increase in blessings, it is of kinds. Among them are spiritual blessings and among them are physical blessings. As for spiritual blessings, the grateful person is always contemplating the kinds of Allah's blessings and the varieties of His grace and generosity. Whoever's kindness to a man is great, that man will inevitably love him. Thus occupying the soul with contemplating the varieties of Allah's grace and kindness necessarily produces a strengthening of the servant's love for Allah the Exalted. The station of love is the highest station of the truthful (ṣiddīqīn, the sincerely faithful ones). Then the servant may advance from that state until his love for the Benefactor becomes so absorbing that he no longer turns to the blessing itself. There is no doubt that the source of all happiness and the sign of all goodness is love of Allah the Exalted and knowledge of Him. Thus it is established that occupying oneself with gratitude produces an increase in spiritual blessings. As for an increase in physical blessings, this is because induction has shown that the more a person occupies himself with thanking Allah's blessings, the more Allah's blessings reach him. In sum, gratitude has its place only because it is an occupation with knowing the One worshipped, and every station that moves the servant from the world of delusion to the world of holiness is the noble, exalted station which produces happiness in religion and in this world.

As for His saying: ﴿But if you are ungrateful, indeed My punishment is severe﴾, what is meant by it is ingratitude (kufrān), not disbelief (kufr). This is because the disbelief mentioned in contrast to gratitude is nothing other than ingratitude. The reason for this is that ingratitude toward a blessing occurs only when one is ignorant that that blessing is a blessing from Allah. Whoever is ignorant of it is ignorant of Allah, and ignorance of Allah is among the greatest kinds of punishment and torment. Moreover, there is here another subtle point: everything other than the One, the Unique, the True, is possible in its essence (mumkin li-dhātihi), and everything possible in its essence comes into existence only through the bringing-into-being of the Necessary in its essence (wājib li-dhātihi), and its non-existence occurs only through the annihilation by the Necessary in its essence. Since this is so, everything other than the Truth is submissive to the Truth and obedient to Him. When all possible things are submissive to the Truth, the Glorified, then in any heart in which the light of knowledge of the Truth and the nobility of His majesty is present, everything else submits to the owner of that heart, because the presence of that light in the heart naturally makes everything else its servant. When the heart is empty of that light, it weakens and becomes base, so everything else makes use of it, and everything different from it despises it. By this intuitive path, the knowledge is attained that occupying oneself with knowing the Truth necessitates the opening of the doors of good in this world and the Hereafter. As for turning away from knowing the Truth by occupying oneself merely with physical things, it necessitates the opening of the doors of calamities and fears in this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verses 8–9:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Moses said: If you disbelieve, you and everyone on earth together, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, and ʿAd, and Thamud, and those after them, whom none knows except Allah? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they put their hands to their mouths and said: "Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent, and indeed we are in grave doubt about that to which you invite us."﴾

Know that when Moses, peace be upon him, explained that occupying oneself with gratitude brings about the increase of good in this world and the Hereafter, and occupying oneself with ingratitude for blessings brings severe punishment and the arrival of calamities in this world and the Hereafter, he then explained that the benefits of gratitude and the harms of ingratitude return only to the one who is grateful and the one who is ungrateful. As for the One who is worshipped and thanked, He is exalted above benefiting from gratitude or being harmed by ingratitude. Therefore, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Moses said: If you disbelieve, you and everyone on earth together, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy.﴾ The purpose of this is to show that Allah the Exalted only commanded these acts of obedience for benefits returning to the worshipper, not for benefits returning to the One worshipped. What indicates that the matter is so is what Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is Free of need﴾. Its explanation is that He is necessarily existent in His essence, and necessarily existent according to all His attributes and considerations. For if He were not necessarily existent in His essence, the preponderance of His existence over non-existence would require a preponderant (murajjih), and so He would not be Free of need; but we have supposed Him Free of need, so this is a contradiction. Thus it is established that His being Free of need necessitates that He is necessarily existent in His essence. And when it is established that He is necessarily existent in His essence, He is also necessarily existent according to all His perfections, for if His essence were not sufficient for the attainment of that perfection, He would require for the attainment of that perfection a separate cause, and then He would not be Free of need; but we have supposed Him Free of need, so this is a contradiction. Thus it is established that His essence is sufficient for the attainment of all His perfections. And when the matter is so, He is Praiseworthy in His essence; for there is no meaning of "Praiseworthy" except one who deserves praise. Thus it is established by this demonstration which we have mentioned that His being Free of need and Praiseworthy requires that He does not increase by the gratitude of the grateful, nor decrease by the ingratitude of the ungrateful. For this meaning He said: ﴿If you disbelieve, you and everyone on earth together, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy.﴾ And these meanings are among the subtle secrets.

Know that our saying: ﴿If you disbelieve, you and everyone on earth together﴾, whether it is understood as disbelief that is the opposite of faith or as ingratitude that is the opposite of thankfulness, the meaning does not differ at all, for He, the Exalted, is Free of need of the worlds in His perfections and in all the attributes of His greatness and majesty.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, and ʿAd, and Thamud﴾. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani mentioned that it is possible that this is an address from Moses, peace be upon him, to his people, and the purpose of it is that he, peace be upon him, was warning them with the like of the destruction of those who came before. It is also possible that it is an address from Allah, the Exalted, through the tongue of Moses to his people, reminding them of the affair of the earlier generations. The aim is only to derive a lesson from the circumstances of those who came before, and this aim is achieved under both interpretations, except that the majority held that it is the beginning of an address to the people of the Messenger ﷺ.

Know that He, the Exalted, mentioned three peoples: the people of Noah, ʿAd, and Thamud.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those after them, whom none knows except Allah﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf mentioned two possibilities regarding it:

The first: that His saying ﴿and those after them, whom none knows except Allah﴾ is a sentence of subject and predicate that has come as a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ).

The second: that it is said: His saying ﴿and those after them﴾ is conjoined to "the people of Noah, ʿAd, and Thamud," and His saying ﴿whom none knows except Allah﴾ has two views:

The first view: that what is meant is that none knows the full extent of their measures except Allah, because what is mentioned in the Qur'an is a summary, while the number, the lifespan, the manner and the quantity are not known.

The second view: that what is meant is the mention of peoples whose reports have not reached us at all, who denied messengers whom we do not know at all, and whom none knows except Allah. Those who hold this second view have criticized the view of those who trace lineages back to Adam, peace be upon him. Ibn Masʿud, when he recited this verse, would say: "The genealogists have lied," meaning that they claim knowledge of genealogies while Allah has denied that knowledge to the servants. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Between ʿAdnan and Ismaʿil there are thirty fathers who are not known." A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And generations between them, many﴾ [al-Furqan: 38], and His saying: ﴿Of them are those We have related to you, and of them are those We have not related to you﴾ [Ghafir: 78]. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that in his genealogy he did not go beyond Maʿadd ibn ʿAdnan ibn Udad, and he said: "Learn from your genealogies that by which you maintain your kinship ties, and learn from the stars that by which you are guided on the way." The judge (al-Qadi) said: On this view it is not possible to be certain of the number of years from Adam, peace be upon him, until this time; for if that were possible, it would not be far-fetched to acquire knowledge of the connected lineages either.

If it is asked: Which of the two views is preferable?

We say: The second view is closer in my opinion, because His saying ﴿none knows them except Allah﴾ negates knowledge of them, and that requires negating knowledge of their very persons; for if their persons were known, and what was unknown were the durations of their lifespans and the manner of their attributes, it would not be correct to negate knowledge of their persons. And since the apparent meaning of the verse is evidence for negating knowledge of their persons, the second view is necessarily closer. Then He, the Exalted, related of these peoples mentioned earlier that when their messengers came to them with clear proofs and miracles, they did several things:

The first of them is His saying: ﴿So they put their hands to their mouths﴾, and regarding its meaning there are two views:

The first: that by the hand and the mouth is meant the well-known limbs.

The second: that by them is meant something other than these two organs, and they were mentioned figuratively and by extension. As for the one who holds the first view, there are three aspects:

The first aspect: that the pronoun in ﴿their hands﴾ and ﴿their mouths﴾ refers to the disbelievers. On this there are several possibilities:

The first: that the disbelievers put their hands to their mouths, biting them out of rage and vexation, from their intense aversion to seeing the messengers and hearing their speech. A parallel is His saying: ﴿They bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾ [Al ʿImran: 119]. This view is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud, may Allah have mercy on them, and it is the choice of al-Qadi.

The second: that when they heard the speech of the prophets they marveled at it and laughed in mockery, and at that point they put their hands to their mouths as one does who is overcome by laughter and places his hand over his mouth.

The third: that they placed their hands over their mouths, gesturing to the prophets to cease this speech and be silent about this talk. This is related from al-Kalbi.

The fourth: that they gestured with their hands to their tongues and to what they had spoken, namely their saying: "Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent"; that is, this is our answer to what you have said, and we have no other, thus despairing them of acceptance. Do you not see His saying: ﴿So they put their hands to their mouths and said: Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾?

The second aspect: that the two pronouns refer to the messengers, peace be upon them, and on this there are two views:

The first: that the disbelievers took the hands of the messengers and placed them over their mouths to silence them and cut off their speech.

The second: that when the messengers despaired of them, they fell silent and placed their own hands over their own mouths; for one who mentions a statement among a people who deny it and whom he fears, that speaker may place his own hand over his own mouth, intending to let them know that he will never return to that statement.

The third aspect: that the pronoun in "their hands" refers to the disbelievers, and in "the mouths" to the messengers, and on this there are two views:

The first: that when the disbelievers heard the admonition, advice and speech of the prophets, peace be upon them, they gestured with their hands toward the mouths of the messengers, in denial and rejection of them.

The second: that the disbelievers placed their hands over the mouths of the prophets, peace be upon them, to prevent them from speaking; and one who goes to great lengths to prevent another from speaking may be treated in this way. As for the second view, namely that mention of the hand and the mouth is extension and metaphor, there are several aspects:

The first aspect: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: By "the hand" is meant what the messengers uttered of proofs, because conveying a proof is a great favor, and a favor is called a "hand." It is said: "So-and-so has a hand (yad) with me" when he has done him a kindness. The hand may also be mentioned while meaning the transaction of a sale or a contract, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you, they are pledging allegiance only to Allah; the hand of Allah is above their hands﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. So the clear proofs which the prophets, peace be upon them, mentioned and established are favors and bounties; and likewise the covenants which they brought to the people are bounties. The plural of "yad" in small numbers is "aydi," and in large numbers "ayadi." Thus it is established that the clear proofs of the prophets, peace be upon them, and their covenants may rightly be called "hands." And since counsel and covenants only come forth from the mouth, when they are not accepted they become returned to where they came from. A parallel is His saying: ﴿When you received it with your tongues and said with your mouths what you had no knowledge of﴾ [al-Nur: 15]. Since acceptance was a receiving with the mouths from the mouths, rejection was a returning into the mouths. This is the complete statement of Abu Muslim in establishing this aspect.

The second aspect: Muhammad ibn Jarir related from some of them that the meaning of His saying ﴿so they put their hands into their mouths﴾ is that they fell silent and gave no answer. It is said of a man who withholds an answer: "He put his hand into his mouth." The Arabs say: "I spoke to so-and-so about a need, and he put his hand into his mouth," when he fell silent and did not reply. Then he (Ibn Jarir) rejected this view and said: They answered with denial, for they said: ﴿Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾.

The third aspect: that by "the hands" is meant the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, upon them, outward and inward; and when they denied the prophets, they exposed those blessings to removal and nullification. So His saying ﴿so they put their hands into their mouths﴾ means: they turned away the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, from themselves by the words that came out of their mouths. It is not far-fetched to take "fi" (in) in the sense of "bi" (with), for prepositions may not be barred from standing in place of one another.

The second kind of the things which Allah, the Exalted, related of the disbelievers is their saying: ﴿Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾, and the meaning is: we disbelieve in that which you claim Allah sent you with, for they did not acknowledge that they had been sent.

Know that the first stage was that they fell silent, refusing to accept the words of the prophets, peace be upon them, and tried to silence the prophets from that claim. The second stage is that they declared outright that they disbelieved in that mission.

The third kind is their saying: ﴿And indeed we are in grave doubt about that to which you invite us﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf said: It is also read "tad'ununa" with the nun assimilated. ﴿Murib﴾ means causing suspicion, or one possessing suspicion, from arabahu; and ar-riba is the unease of the soul and the failure to be at rest with a matter.

If it is asked: When they mentioned in the second stage that they disbelieved in their mission, how do they then mention after that that they were doubtful and uneasy about the correctness of their statement?

We say: It is as if they said: Either we are disbelievers in your mission, or, if we do not abandon this certainty and conviction, then at the least we are doubtful and uneasy about the correctness of your prophethood. And on either supposition there is no way to acknowledge your prophethood. And Allah knows best.

The second: that it is said: His saying ﴿and those after them﴾ is conjoined to "the people of Noah, ʿAd, and Thamud," and His saying ﴿whom none knows except Allah﴾ has two views:

The first view: that what is meant is that none knows the full extent of their measures except Allah, because what is mentioned in the Qur'an is a summary, while the number, the lifespan, the manner and the quantity are not known.

The second view: that what is meant is the mention of peoples whose reports have not reached us at all, who denied messengers whom we do not know at all, and whom none knows except Allah. Those who hold this second view have criticized the view of those who trace lineages back to Adam, peace be upon him. Ibn Masʿud, when he recited this verse, would say: "The genealogists have lied," meaning that they claim knowledge of genealogies while Allah has denied that knowledge to the servants. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Between ʿAdnan and Ismaʿil there are thirty fathers who are not known." A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And generations between them, many﴾ [al-Furqan: 38], and His saying: ﴿Of them are those We have related to you, and of them are those We have not related to you﴾ [Ghafir: 78]. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that in his genealogy he did not go beyond Maʿadd ibn ʿAdnan ibn Udad, and he said: "Learn from your genealogies that by which you maintain your kinship ties, and learn from the stars that by which you are guided on the way." The judge (al-Qadi) said: On this view it is not possible to be certain of the number of years from Adam, peace be upon him, until this time; for if that were possible, it would not be far-fetched to acquire knowledge of the connected lineages either.

If it is asked: Which of the two views is preferable?

We say: The second view is closer in my opinion, because His saying ﴿none knows them except Allah﴾ negates knowledge of them, and that requires negating knowledge of their very persons; for if their persons were known, and what was unknown were the durations of their lifespans and the manner of their attributes, it would not be correct to negate knowledge of their persons. And since the apparent meaning of the verse is evidence for negating knowledge of their persons, the second view is necessarily closer. Then He, the Exalted, related of these peoples mentioned earlier that when their messengers came to them with clear proofs and miracles, they did several things:

The first of them is His saying: ﴿So they put their hands to their mouths﴾, and regarding its meaning there are two views:

The first: that by the hand and the mouth is meant the well-known limbs.

The second: that by them is meant something other than these two organs, and they were mentioned figuratively and by extension. As for the one who holds the first view, there are three aspects:

The first aspect: that the pronoun in ﴿their hands﴾ and ﴿their mouths﴾ refers to the disbelievers. On this there are several possibilities:

The first: that the disbelievers put their hands to their mouths, biting them out of rage and vexation, from their intense aversion to seeing the messengers and hearing their speech. A parallel is His saying: ﴿They bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾ [Al ʿImran: 119]. This view is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud, may Allah have mercy on them, and it is the choice of al-Qadi.

The second: that when they heard the speech of the prophets they marveled at it and laughed in mockery, and at that point they put their hands to their mouths as one does who is overcome by laughter and places his hand over his mouth.

The third: that they placed their hands over their mouths, gesturing to the prophets to cease this speech and be silent about this talk. This is related from al-Kalbi.

The fourth: that they gestured with their hands to their tongues and to what they had spoken, namely their saying: "Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent"; that is, this is our answer to what you have said, and we have no other, thus despairing them of acceptance. Do you not see His saying: ﴿So they put their hands to their mouths and said: Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾?

The second aspect: that the two pronouns refer to the messengers, peace be upon them, and on this there are two views:

The first: that the disbelievers took the hands of the messengers and placed them over their mouths to silence them and cut off their speech.

The second: that when the messengers despaired of them, they fell silent and placed their own hands over their own mouths; for one who mentions a statement among a people who deny it and whom he fears, that speaker may place his own hand over his own mouth, intending to let them know that he will never return to that statement.

The third aspect: that the pronoun in "their hands" refers to the disbelievers, and in "the mouths" to the messengers, and on this there are two views:

The first: that when the disbelievers heard the admonition, advice and speech of the prophets, peace be upon them, they gestured with their hands toward the mouths of the messengers, in denial and rejection of them.

The second: that the disbelievers placed their hands over the mouths of the prophets, peace be upon them, to prevent them from speaking; and one who goes to great lengths to prevent another from speaking may be treated in this way. As for the second view, namely that mention of the hand and the mouth is extension and metaphor, there are several aspects:

The first aspect: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: By "the hand" is meant what the messengers uttered of proofs, because conveying a proof is a great favor, and a favor is called a "hand." It is said: "So-and-so has a hand (yad) with me" when he has done him a kindness. The hand may also be mentioned while meaning the transaction of a sale or a contract, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you, they are pledging allegiance only to Allah; the hand of Allah is above their hands﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. So the clear proofs which the prophets, peace be upon them, mentioned and established are favors and bounties; and likewise the covenants which they brought to the people are bounties. The plural of "yad" in small numbers is "aydi," and in large numbers "ayadi." Thus it is established that the clear proofs of the prophets, peace be upon them, and their covenants may rightly be called "hands." And since counsel and covenants only come forth from the mouth, when they are not accepted they become returned to where they came from. A parallel is His saying: ﴿When you received it with your tongues and said with your mouths what you had no knowledge of﴾ [al-Nur: 15]. Since acceptance was a receiving with the mouths from the mouths, rejection was a returning into the mouths. This is the complete statement of Abu Muslim in establishing this aspect.

The second aspect: Muhammad ibn Jarir related from some of them that the meaning of His saying ﴿so they put their hands into their mouths﴾ is that they fell silent and gave no answer. It is said of a man who withholds an answer: "He put his hand into his mouth." The Arabs say: "I spoke to so-and-so about a need, and he put his hand into his mouth," when he fell silent and did not reply. Then he (Ibn Jarir) rejected this view and said: They answered with denial, for they said: ﴿Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾.

The third aspect: that by "the hands" is meant the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, upon them, outward and inward; and when they denied the prophets, they exposed those blessings to removal and nullification. So His saying ﴿so they put their hands into their mouths﴾ means: they turned away the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, from themselves by the words that came out of their mouths. It is not far-fetched to take "fi" (in) in the sense of "bi" (with), for prepositions may not be barred from standing in place of one another.

The second kind of the things which Allah, the Exalted, related of the disbelievers is their saying: ﴿Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾, and the meaning is: we disbelieve in that which you claim Allah sent you with, for they did not acknowledge that they had been sent.

Know that the first stage was that they fell silent, refusing to accept the words of the prophets, peace be upon them, and tried to silence the prophets from that claim. The second stage is that they declared outright that they disbelieved in that mission.

The third kind is their saying: ﴿And indeed we are in grave doubt about that to which you invite us﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf said: It is also read "tad'ununa" with the nun assimilated. ﴿Murib﴾ means causing suspicion, or one possessing suspicion, from arabahu; and ar-riba is the unease of the soul and the failure to be at rest with a matter.

If it is asked: When they mentioned in the second stage that they disbelieved in their mission, how do they then mention after that that they were doubtful and uneasy about the correctness of their statement?

We say: It is as if they said: Either we are disbelievers in your mission, or, if we do not abandon this certainty and conviction, then at the least we are doubtful and uneasy about the correctness of your prophethood. And on either supposition there is no way to acknowledge your prophethood. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verse 10 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Their messengers said: "Is there doubt about God, the Originator of the heavens and the earth? He calls you so that He may forgive you some of your sins and grant you respite until a specified term." They said: "You are only human beings like us. You wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship, so bring us a clear authority."﴾

Know that when those disbelievers said to the messengers: ﴿Indeed, we are in disquieting doubt about that to which you invite us﴾, their messengers replied: "Do you doubt God, and His being the Originator of the heavens and the earth, and the Originator of our souls, our spirits, our provisions, and all our welfare? We only invite you to worship this Bounteous God, and we only forbid you from worshipping others besides Him. Clear reason testifies to the soundness of these meanings, so how could you say: ﴿Indeed, we are in disquieting doubt about that to which you invite us﴾?" This arrangement is extremely fine. There are several issues in the verse.

The first issue: His saying, ﴿Is there doubt about God?﴾ is an interrogation in the form of denial. When He mentioned this meaning, He followed it with the proof that indicates the existence of the Creator who chooses, which is His saying: ﴿the Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾. We have mentioned in this book how the existence of the heavens and the earth indicates their need for a Creator who chooses and is wise, many times and in various ways, so we will not repeat it here.

The second issue: The author of the *Kashshaf* said: The interrogative hamzah of denial has been placed before the adverbial phrase (*zarf*), because the discussion is not about doubt itself, but about the fact that God's existence does not admit of doubt. I say: Some people have held that before reaching the subtle proofs, innate nature (*fitrah*) testifies to the existence of the Creator who chooses. Several points show that the primary innate nature testifies to this:

The first point: Some wise people have said: Whoever slaps a child on the face, that slap indicates the existence of a Creator, the obligation of commands, the obligation of a Day of Recompense, and the necessity of a prophet. As for its indication of the existence of the Creator who chooses, it is because when a sensible child is struck on the face, he cries out and says: "Who struck me?" This is only because the testimony of his nature indicates that, since the slap came into being after it did not exist, its coming into being must be due to an agent who did it, and to a chooser who brought it into existence. Since the original nature testifies to the dependence of that event, despite its smallness and insignificance, on an agent, then it is even more fitting that it should testify to the dependence of all events in the world on an agent. As for its indication of the obligation of commands, it is because that child cries out and calls, saying: "Why did that striker strike me?" This indicates that his nature testifies that human actions fall under command and prohibition, and are included within obligation, and that a human being was not created to do whatever act he wishes and desires. As for its indication of the obligation of the Day of Recompense, the child seeks retribution for that slap, and as long as it is possible for him to seek that retribution, he does not give it up. Since the original nature testifies to the obligation of retribution for that small deed, it is even more fitting that it should testify to the obligation of retribution for all deeds. As for its indication of the necessity of prophethood, it is because people need someone who explains to them how much punishment is due for that degree of offense. There is no meaning to a prophet except a human being who determines these matters and explains these rulings to them. Thus it is established that the innate reason of human nature judges that a human being must have these four matters.

The second point, in alerting to the fact that acknowledging the existence of the Creator is self-evident: The innate nature testifies that the coming into being of a house decorated with wondrous designs, built on subtle arrangements that suit wisdom and benefit, is impossible except in the presence of a knowing painter and a wise builder. It is known that the traces of wisdom in the upper and lower worlds are more numerous than the traces of wisdom in that small house. Since the original nature testifies that the design requires a designer and the building requires a builder, it is even more fitting that it should testify that this whole world requires a wise agent who chooses.

The third point: When a person falls into severe distress and a strong calamity, hope of help from anyone no longer remains in his mind. He, by the very origin of his creation and the requirement of his disposition, implores the One who will deliver him from it and bring him out of its entanglements and snares. This is nothing but the testimony of the innate nature to its need for the Creator who manages affairs.

The fourth point: Every existent is either independent of an influencer or not. If it is independent of an influencer, then it is the Necessary Existent in Itself, for there is no meaning to "necessary in itself" except an existent that has no need of anything else. If it is not independent of an influencer, then it is in need, and what is in need must have something on which it depends, and that is the Creator who chooses.

The fifth point: Acknowledging the existence of a God who chooses and who imposes obligations, and the existence of the Return, is more cautious. Therefore it is necessary to turn to it. These are four ranks:

The first: Acknowledging the existence of God is more cautious, because if He does not exist, there is no harm in acknowledging His existence; and if He does exist, then denying Him incurs the greatest harms.

The second: Acknowledging that He is an agent who chooses, because if He were a mere necessitating cause, there would be no harm in acknowledging that He chooses; but if He chooses, then denying that He chooses incurs the greatest harms.

The third: Acknowledging that He has imposed obligations on His servants, because if He has imposed no obligation on any of His servants, there is no harm in believing that He imposed obligations on the servants; but if He did impose them, then denying those obligations incurs the greatest harms.

The fourth: Acknowledging the existence of the Return. If the truth is that there is no Return, there is no harm in acknowledging it, because one would lose only these bodily pleasures, which are base and deficient. If the truth is the obligation of the Return, then denying it incurs the greatest harms. Thus it is clear that acknowledging these stations is more cautious, and therefore it is necessary to turn to it, because the self-evident judgment of reason is that harm must be averted from the self to the extent possible.

[p. 74]

* * *

The third issue: When He established the proof of God's existence by the argument that He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, He described Him with perfect mercy, generosity, and bounty, and demonstrated this in two ways:

The first: His saying: ﴿He calls you so that He may forgive you some of your sins.﴾ The author of the *Kashshaf* said: If someone asks, "What is the meaning of partitive *min* (some) in His saying ﴿some of your sins﴾?" then he answers: It has come in this form only in addressing the disbelievers, as in His saying: ﴿Worship God, fear Him, and obey me﴾ ﴿He will forgive you some of your sins﴾ [Nuh: 3], and ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of God and believe in Him; He will forgive you some of your sins﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31]. And in addressing the believers He said: ﴿Shall I direct you to a commerce that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ [al-Saff: 10], up to His saying ﴿He will forgive you your sins﴾ [al-Saff: 12]. Induction indicates the soundness of what we have mentioned. Then he said: It seems that this is to distinguish between the two addresses, and so that the two groups are not equated in the Return. It has also been said that he meant that He forgives them what is between them and God, unlike what is between them and the servants of injustices. This is the statement of this man.

Al-Wahidi said in *al-Basit*: Abu 'Ubayda said that [*min*] is extra. Sibawayh denied its being extra in an obligatory context. If we say it is not extra, then there are two views here:

One: Part is mentioned here while the whole is intended, by way of extension.

The second: *min* here indicates substitution, meaning that forgiveness is a substitute for sins. So *min* enters because forgiveness includes the sense of substitution for evil deeds.

Al-Qadi said: al-Asamm mentioned that the word *min* here indicates partiality, meaning that when you repent, He forgives you the sins that are among the major ones. As for those that are among the minor ones, there is no need to forgive them, because in themselves they are forgiven. Al-Qadi said: He has gone too far in this interpretation, because the minor sins of disbelievers are like their major sins in that they are not forgiven except by repentance. A minor sin is forgiven only for believing monotheists, in that their reward exceeds its punishment. As for one who has no reward at all, none of his sins is minor, and none of them is forgiven. Then he said: There is another view, namely that the disbeliever may forget some of his sins at the time of his repentance and turning back, so that what is forgiven of them is only what he mentioned and repented of. This is the sum of what people have said about this word.

* * *

The fourth issue: I say this verse indicates that God may forgive sins without repentance for the people of faith. The evidence for this is that He said: ﴿He calls you so that He may forgive you some of your sins.﴾ He promised the forgiveness of some sins absolutely, without the condition of repentance. Therefore He must forgive some sins absolutely, without repentance. That portion is not disbelief, because there is a consensus (*ijma'*) that God does not forgive disbelief except by repentance from it and entering faith. Therefore the portion He forgives without repentance must be other sins than disbelief.

If it is said: Why could it not be said that *min* is superfluous, as Abu 'Ubayda said; or we say that by "some" here is meant "all," as al-Wahidi said; or we say that it means the replacement of an evil deed with a good one, as al-Wahidi also said; or we say that it means distinguishing the believer from the disbeliever in address, as the author of the *Kashshaf* said; or we say that it means restricting this forgiveness to major sins, as al-Asamm said; or we say that it means the sins that the disbeliever mentions upon entering faith, as al-Qadi said? We reply: All these views are weak. As for the claim that it is superfluous, its meaning is to judge a word of God's speech as an empty, corrupt excess, and a rational person does not permit resorting to this without necessity. As for al-Wahidi's statement that the word *min* here means "all," it is the very same as what Abu 'Ubayda said, because its conclusion is that His saying ﴿that He may forgive you some of your sins﴾ means that He forgives you your sins, and this is exactly what he reported from Abu 'Ubayda, and it is reported that Sibawayh denied it. As for

[p. 75]

his saying that it means the replacement of an evil deed with a good one, there is nothing in the language to show that the word *min* indicates substitution. As for the statement of the author of the *Kashshaf* that it means distinguishing the address to the believer from the address to the disbeliever by additional honor, it is of the kind of empty boasting, because if this partiality exists, there is no need to mention this answer, and if it does not exist, this answer is false. As for al-Asamm's view, its refutation has already preceded. As for al-Qadi's view, his reply is that when a disbeliever becomes a Muslim, all his sins become forgiven, due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The one who repents of a sin is like one who has no sin." Thus it is established that all the interpretations they mentioned are far-fetched and invalid. Rather, what is meant is what we have mentioned: that He forgives some of his sins without repentance, namely what is other than disbelief. As for disbelief, it is also among the sins, and He forgives it only by repentance. Since it is established that He forgives the major sins of a disbeliever without repentance, on the condition that he comes with faith, then it is even more fitting that this state should be attained by a believer. This is what came to mind extemporaneously. And God knows the reality of the matter best.

The second kind of what God promised in this verse is His saying: ﴿and grant you respite until a specified term.﴾ On this there are two views:

The first: The meaning is that if you believe, God will delay your death until a specified term; otherwise He will hasten upon you a punishment of annihilation.

The second: Ibn 'Abbas said: The meaning is that He will let you enjoy good things and pleasures in this world until death.

If it is said: Did He not say: ﴿When their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34]? How then does He say here: ﴿and grant you respite until a specified term﴾?

We have already discussed this matter in Surah al-An'am, in His saying: ﴿Then He decreed a term, and a term specified with Him﴾ [al-An'am: 2]. Then God Most High related that when the messengers had mentioned these things to those disbelievers, they said: ﴿You are only human beings like us. You wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship, so bring us a clear authority.﴾

Know that this statement contains three kinds of doubts (shubah):

The first doubt: human individuals are equal in their complete quiddity (mahiyyah), so it is impossible that the disparity among these individuals should reach this degree, namely that one of them be a messenger from God, informed of the unseen, in company with the host of angels, while the rest are heedless of all these states. They also said: if you have parted from us in these lofty, sublime divine states, then it follows that you must part from us in the lowly states, such as the need for eating, drinking, relieving oneself, and sexual intercourse. This doubt is what is meant by their saying: ﴿You are only human beings like us.﴾

The second doubt: adherence to the way of imitation (taqlid). They found their fathers, their scholars and their elders in unanimous agreement upon the worship of idols. They said: it is far-fetched to say that those ancients, despite their numbers and the strength of their minds, did not recognise the falsehood of this religion, while a single man recognised its corruption and came to know its invalidity. The common people, perhaps, added to this matter another statement: when a learned man demonstrates the weakness of the words of some of the earlier generations, they say to him: your speech would only appear correct if the earlier ones were present; as for debating with the dead, that is easy. This is a statement mentioned by fools and the rabble, and those disbelievers also mentioned it. This doubt is what is meant by His saying: ﴿You wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship.﴾

The third doubt: they said that a miracle (mu'jiz) does not indicate truthfulness at all. Although they conceded that a miracle indicates truthfulness, they criticised what those messengers brought, claiming that these were ordinary matters and not of the kind of miracles that lie beyond human power. The saying ﴿so bring us a clear authority﴾ alludes to this kind of doubt.

This is the explanation of this verse to the best of our capacity. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verses 11–12:

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Their messengers said to them: "We are only human beings like you, but God bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants. It is not for us to bring you an authority except by God's leave. And upon God let the believers rely."﴾ ﴿"And why should we not rely upon God, when He has guided us to our paths? We will surely bear patiently whatever harm you inflict upon us. And upon God let those who rely (upon Him) rely."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, related the doubts of the disbelievers in their criticism of prophethood, He related the answers of the prophets, peace be upon them, to them.

As for the first doubt, which is their saying: ﴿You are only human beings like us﴾, its answer is that the prophets agreed that the matter is as they said, but they explained that similarity in humanity and mankind does not prevent some humans from being singled out for the rank of prophethood, because this rank is one that God bestows upon whomever He wills of His servants. If that is so, then this doubt has fallen away.

Know also that this station contains a noble, subtle investigation: a group of the sages of Islam (ḥukamāʾ, philosophers) said that a person who is not specially endowed in his soul and body with sublime, heavenly, holy qualities, it is rationally impossible for the attribute of prophethood to be realised in him. As for the Ẓāhirīs among the People of the Sunnah and the Community, they claimed that attaining prophethood is a gift from God Most High, which He grants to whomever He wills of His servants, and its attainment does not depend on that person being distinguished from the rest of people by an excess of spiritual illumination and holy power. These people held fast to this verse, for He, exalted is He, made clear that attaining prophethood is nothing but by pure favour from God Most High and a gift from Him. The discourse on this subject is obscure, deep and subtle. The earlier scholars answered this by saying that they did not mention their soul-related and bodily virtues out of humility, and they confined themselves to their saying: ﴿But God bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾ [Ibrahim: 11], with prophethood, because He knew that He does not single them out with those honours unless they are characterised by the virtues for the sake of which they deserved that distinction, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124].

As for the second doubt, which is their saying: the consensus of the predecessors upon that religion indicates that it is true, because it is unlikely that something would become apparent to one man that has not become apparent to a great multitude. Its answer is the very same answer given to the first doubt, because the distinguishing between truth and falsehood, and between truthfulness and lying, is a gift from God Most High and a bounty from Him, and it is not unlikely that He singles out some of His servants with this gift and withholds it from a great multitude.

As for the third doubt, which is their saying: We are not content with these miracles you have brought, and we only want overpowering, mighty miracles.

Page 77
The answer to it is His saying: ﴿It is not for us to bring you an authority except by God's leave.﴾ The explanation of this answer is that the miracle we have brought and held fast to is a decisive proof, a conclusive clear evidence and a complete demonstration. As for the things you have requested, they are additional matters, and the judgment concerning them belongs to God Most High: if He creates and manifests them, then the favour is His, and if He does not create them, then the justice is His, and no judgment is passed against Him after the manifestation of the sufficient measure. Then He, exalted is He, related that the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, said after that: ﴿And upon God let the believers rely.﴾ The apparent meaning is that when the prophets answered their doubts with that answer, the people turned to foolishness, threats and intimidation. At this, the prophets, peace be upon them, said: We do not fear your intimidation nor do we heed your threats, for our reliance is upon God and our dependence is upon God's grace. Perhaps God, glorified is He, had revealed to them that those disbelievers cannot inflict evil or harm upon them. And even if this revelation had not occurred, it is not unlikely that they would not heed their foolishness, because their spirits were radiant with divine knowledge, illuminated by the lights of the unseen world, and whenever the soul is characterised by these qualities, it rarely cares about bodily conditions and rarely gives them any weight in states of ease and hardship, or in times of severity and prosperity. For this reason they relied upon God, depended upon God's grace, and cut off their hopes from all but God.

What indicates that the intended meaning is what we have mentioned is His saying, relating about them: ﴿And why should we not rely upon God, when He has guided us to our paths? We will surely bear patiently whatever harm you inflict upon us.﴾ That is, since He has singled us out with these spiritual ranks and divine, lordly knowledge, how is it fitting for us not to rely upon God? Rather, what befits us is that we rely upon none but Him and depend upon none but Him in attaining our aims, for whoever has attained the honour of servanthood and reached the station of sincerity and unveiling, it is disgraceful for him to turn, in any matter, to other than the Real, whether it be a king, an angel, a spirit or a body. This verse indicates that He, exalted is He, protects His sincere friends in His servanthood from the plots and schemes of their enemies.

Then they said: ﴿We will surely bear patiently whatever harm you inflict upon us﴾, for patience is the key to relief and the dawn of good things, and the truth must inevitably become dominant and overpowering, and falsehood must inevitably become defeated and subdued. Then they repeated their saying: ﴿And upon God let those who rely (upon Him) rely.﴾ The benefit of this is that they commanded themselves to rely upon God in His saying: ﴿And why should we not rely upon God﴾; then, when they had finished with themselves, they commanded their followers with that, saying: ﴿And upon God let those who rely (upon Him) rely.﴾ This indicates that the speech of one who commands good does not have effect unless he first does that good himself. I have seen in the words of Shaykh Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, a fine discourse, and its summary is: a person is either deficient or perfect or free of both attributes. As for the deficient, he is either deficient in his own self but does not strive to diminish the condition of others, or he is deficient and at the same time strives to diminish the condition of others. The first is the one who goes astray, and the second is the misguided misleader. As for the perfect, he is either perfect but unable to perfect others, and these are the friends of God, or he is perfect and able to perfect the deficient, and these are the prophets. For this reason, he, peace be upon him, said: "The scholars of my community are like the prophets of the Children of Israel."

Since the degrees of deficiency and perfection, and the degrees of perfecting and misleading, are unlimited in terms of quantity and quality, the degrees of sainthood and life are necessarily unlimited in terms of perfection and deficiency. So the friend (walī) is the perfect human being who is not able to perfect others, and the prophet is the perfect human being who perfects others. Then his spiritual and soul-related power may be sufficient to perfect two deficient persons, and it may be stronger than that, sufficing to perfect ten or a hundred, and that power may be dominant and mighty, affecting the world like the sun, turning the spirits of most of the people of the world from the station of ignorance to the station of knowledge, and from seeking the world to seeking the Hereafter. Such was the spirit of Muhammad ﷺ, for at the time of his appearance the world was filled with Jews, most of whom were anthropomorphists (mushabbiha), and with Christians, who were incarnationists (ḥulūliyya), and with Magians, whose corrupt doctrines are evident, and with idol-worshippers, whose religion's foolishness is too evident to require explanation. When the call of Muhammad ﷺ appeared, the power of his spirit spread through spirits, and it turned most of the people of the world from polytheism to monotheism, from anthropomorphism to transcendence (tanzīh), and from absorption in seeking the world to turning towards the world of the Hereafter. From this station the reality of prophethood and messengership is unveiled to a human being.

These are lofty secrets stored in the words of the Qur'an, and whoever looks into the knowledge of the Qur'an while being heedless of them is deprived of the secrets of the sciences of the Qur'an. And God knows best.

The first: it was mentioned for initiating reliance (istiḥdāth al-tawakkul).

The second: for striving to preserve it and sustain it. And God knows best.

If that is so, then this doubt has fallen away.

Know also that this station contains a noble, subtle investigation: a group of the sages of Islam (ḥukamāʾ, philosophers) said that a person who is not specially endowed in his soul and body with sublime, heavenly, holy qualities, it is rationally impossible for the attribute of prophethood to be realised in him. As for the Ẓāhirīs among the People of the Sunnah and the Community, they claimed that attaining prophethood is a gift from God Most High, which He grants to whomever He wills of His servants, and its attainment does not depend on that person being distinguished from the rest of people by an excess of spiritual illumination and holy power. As for the third doubt, which is their saying: We are not content with these miracles you have brought, and we only want overpowering, mighty miracles.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verses 13–17 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to their messengers, "We will surely drive you out of our land, or you will return to our religion." So their Lord revealed to them, "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers. And We will surely settle you in the land after them. That is for whoever fears My standing [before Me] and fears My threat."﴾ ﴿And they sought victory, and every obstinate tyrant was disappointed. Ahead of him is Hell, and he will be given to drink of festering water.﴾ ﴿He will gulp it down but will hardly swallow it, and death will come to him from every place, yet he will not die. And ahead of him is a severe punishment.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, related about the prophets, peace be upon them, that they relied, in repelling the evils of their enemies, only on trusting in Him and depending upon His protection and safeguarding, He related about the disbelievers that they went to extremes in foolishness and said: ﴿We will surely drive you out of our land, or you will return to our religion.﴾ The meaning is: one of the two matters will certainly happen without doubt, either your expulsion or your return to our religion (millah, the religious community and creed). The reason for this is that the people of truth in every age are few, while the people of falsehood are many, and the wrongdoers and the sinners cooperate and support one another. For these reasons they were able to utter this foolishness.

If it is said: this implies that they were upon their religion at the beginning, so that they would return to it.

We say: the answer has several aspects.

The first aspect: those prophets, peace be upon them, grew up in those lands and were from those tribes, and at the beginning they did not show opposition to those disbelievers. Rather, they were outwardly with them without showing any opposition. So the people assumed, for this reason, that they had been upon their religion at the beginning, and for this reason they said: ﴿or you will return to our religion.﴾

The second aspect: this is a report of the words of the disbelievers, and it is not necessary that everything they said be true. Perhaps they imagined that, although the matter was not as they imagined.

The third aspect: perhaps the address, although outwardly directed to the messengers, is actually intended for their followers and companions, and there is no harm in saying that they had been upon the religion of those disbelievers before that time.

The fourth aspect: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "The verb ʿāda (to return) in the sense of 'becoming' is common in the speech of the Arabs."

The fifth aspect: perhaps those prophets were, before their being sent, upon some creed of the creeds, then He, exalted is He, revealed to them the abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of one ruling by a later one) of that creed and commanded them with another law, and the peoples remained upon that law which had become abrogated, persisting in the path of disbelief. On this assumption, it is not far-fetched that they asked the prophets to return to that creed.

The sixth aspect: it is not far-fetched that the meaning is: ﴿or you will return to our religion,﴾ that is, to what you were upon before claiming prophethood, namely silence about criticizing our religion and not confronting it with reproach and denunciation. On all these aspects the question is resolved. And Allah knows best.

Know that when the disbelievers mentioned this statement, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So their Lord revealed to them, "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers. And We will surely settle you in the land after them."﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿We will surely destroy the wrongdoers⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠ ﻿⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ —⁠ ⁠﻿⁠ this is a quotation which requires the implicit supposition of a saying, or treating the revelation as if it were a saying, because it is a kind of saying. Abū Ḥaywa recited: "la-yuhlikanna al-ẓālimīn wa-la-yuskinannakum" with the (yāʾ) prefix, taking into account that "awḥā" (he revealed) is a third-person verb, and this expression is in the third person. A parallel to it is your saying: "Zayd swore that he would surely go out, and I will surely go out." The word "land" means the land of the wrongdoers and their abodes. A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿And We made the people who had been oppressed inherit the eastern and western parts of the land﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 137], and ﴿And He made you inherit their land, their homes﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 27]. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever harms his neighbor, Allah will make him inherit his house." Know that this verse indicates that whoever relies upon his Lord in repelling his enemy, Allah will suffice him against his enemy.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is for whoever fears My standing [before Me] and fears My threat.﴾ His saying "that" is an indication that what Allah, exalted is He, decreed of destroying the wrongdoers and settling the believers in their homes after that matter is true. ﴿That is for whoever fears My standing⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠﻿ ⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠ ⁠﻿ ⁠ ⁠ ⁠ ⁠ —⁠ and regarding this there are several aspects:

The first: the intended meaning is My standing (mawqif), which is the standing of reckoning, because that standing is the standing of Allah, where His servants stand on the Day of Resurrection. A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿But as for one who feared the standing of his Lord﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 40], and His saying: ﴿And for one who feared the standing of his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 46].

The second: the word "maqām" is a verbal noun like "qiyāma"; it is said: "qāma, qiyāman wa-maqāman." Al-Farrāʾ said: "That is for whoever fears My standing over him (qiyāmī ʿalayhi) and My watching over him, like His saying: ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [as one who does not?]⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠﻿ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ —⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠ ﻿⁠

The third: "That is for whoever fears My standing," that is, My upholding of justice and rightness, for He, exalted is He, decides only with truth and judges only with justice, and He, exalted is He, is steadfast upon justice; He never deviates from it and never swerves from it at all.

The fourth: "That is for whoever fears My standing," that is, the standing of one who seeks refuge with Me. This is from the category of the idafa (construct) of a verbal noun to its object.

The fifth: "That is for whoever fears My standing," that is, for whoever fears Me. The mention of "standing" here is like saying: "The peace of Allah upon the high assembly of so-and-so," meaning: the peace of Allah upon so-and-so. So it is the same here.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and fears My threat.﴾ Al-Wāḥidī said: "al-waʿīd is a noun from awʿada, iʿdāʾan, and it means intimidation (tahdīd)." Ibn ʿAbbās said: "He feared what I threatened of punishment."

Know that He, exalted is He, first mentioned His saying: ﴿for whoever fears My standing,⁠﻿⁠ ⁠﻿⁠ then He joined to it His saying: ﴿and fears My threat.﴾ This requires that fear of Allah, exalted is He, be different from fear of Allah's threat. A parallel to it is that love of Allah, exalted is He, is different from love of Allah's reward. This is a noble and lofty station in the secrets of wisdom and affirmation.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And they sought victory,⁠﻿⁠ and in this there are two issues.

The first issue: the verb "istaftaḥū" (they sought victory/judgment) has two meanings here:

One of them: seeking victory through help. So His saying ﴿and they sought victory⁠﻿⁠ means: they sought help from Allah against their enemies. It is like His saying: ﴿If you seek a decision, the decision has certainly come to you﴾ [al-Anfāl: 19].

The second: "al-fatḥ" means judgment and decision. So "istaftaḥū" means: they asked Allah for judgment and sought from Him a decision between them. It is derived from "al-futāḥa," which is arbitration, like His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 89].

Having known this, we say: both opinions were mentioned by the exegetes. On the first opinion, those who sought victory are the messengers, because they sought Allah's help and invoked punishment upon their people when they despaired of their faith. Noah said: ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers a single dweller﴾ [Nūḥ: 26]. Moses said: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth﴾ [Yūnus: 88], the verse. And Lot said: ﴿My Lord, help me against the corrupt people﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 30].

On the third opinion, which is seeking judgment and decision, the more apt view is that those who sought judgment are the nations, because they said: "O Allah, if these messengers are truthful, then punish us." From this is the saying of the disbelievers of Quraysh: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾. And like the saying of others: ﴿Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful﴾.

The second issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: His saying ﴿and they sought victory⁠﻿⁠ is conjoined to His saying ﴿So He revealed to them⁠﻿⁠. It was read as "wa-istaftiḥū" in the imperative form, and it is conjoined to His saying ﴿We will surely destroy⁠﻿⁠, meaning: their Lord revealed to them and said to them: "We will surely destroy," and said to them: "Seek victory."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and every obstinate tyrant was disappointed.⁠﻿⁠ And in this there are two issues:

The first issue: If we say the ones seeking victory are the messengers, the meaning is that the messengers sought victory, were helped, succeeded in their objective, and triumphed, ﴿and every obstinate tyrant was disappointed,⁠﻿⁠ and they are their people. If we say the ones seeking victory are the disbelievers, the meaning is that the disbelievers sought victory against the messengers, thinking that they were upon the truth and the messengers were upon falsehood, ﴿and every obstinate tyrant was disappointed⁠﻿⁠ among them, and he did not prosper by reason of his seeking victory against the messengers.

The second issue: "al-jabbār" here means one who is arrogant toward obeying Allah and worshipping Him. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and he was not a tyrant, disobedient﴾ [Maryam: 14]. Abū ʿUbayda, from al-Aḥmar, said: it is said: "fīhi jabriyya, wa-jabarūwa, wa-jabarūt, wa-jabbūra." Al-Zajjāj related: "al-jibriyya" and "al-jibr" with a kasra on the jīm and the bāʾ, "al-tajbār," and "al-jibriyāʾ." Al-Wāḥidī said: these are eight dialects for the verbal noun of "al-jabbār." In a ḥadīth, a woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he commanded her with a matter, but she refused it. He said: "Leave her, for she is a jabbāra," meaning arrogant. As for "al-ʿanīd," the lexicographers differed about its derivation. Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: "al-ʿunūd" is opposition, distancing, and abandonment. Others said: its root is from "al-ʿinḍ," which is a side; it is said: "fulān yamshī ʿindan," meaning he walks to one side. So the meaning of ʿānada and ʿanada is that he took to one side, turning away; and "ʿānada fulān fulānan" means he kept away from him and was on one side from him.

Having known this, we say: that he is a jabbār, arrogant, indicates the inner moral disposition, and that he is ʿanīd indicates the effect issuing from that disposition, which is that he is distant from the truth and deviates from it. There is no doubt that a person whose disposition is tyranny and arrogance and whose action is ʿunūd, which is deviation from truth and sincerity, is disappointed in all good things and loses all kinds of felicity.

* * *

Know that when He, exalted is He, decreed disappointment for him and described him as a jabbār, ʿanīd, He described the manner of his punishment with several matters:

The first: His saying: ﴿Ahead of him is Hell.⁠﻿⁠ Here there is a difficulty, which is that the intended meaning is "in front of him is Hell," so how can the word "warāʾ" (behind) be applied to what is in front and ahead?

They answered it in several ways:

The first: the word "warāʾ" is a name for what is hidden from you, and both what is in front of you and what is behind you are hidden from you, so applying the word "warāʾ" to each of them is correct. The poet said:

*Perhaps the distress in which I have been living will have relief behind it, close at hand.*

It is also said: death is "warāʾ" (behind/ahead of) everyone.

The second: Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn al-Sikkīt said: "al-warāʾ" is one of the words with opposite meanings, applied to both the behind and the front. The reason for this is that whatever is behind may become in front and vice versa, so it is indeed permissible for the word "warāʾ" to be applied to the front. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there was behind them a king who seized﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], meaning in front of them. It is also said: death is from behind a person.

The third: Ibn al-Anbārī said: "warāʾ" means "baʿda" (after). The poet said:

*And there is no path for a man beyond Allah.*

meaning: there is no path after Allah.

Once this is established, we say: He, exalted is He, decreed disappointment upon him in His saying: ﴿and every obstinate tyrant was disappointed.⁠﻿⁠ Then He said: ﴿Ahead of him is Hell⁠﻿⁠, meaning: after disappointment, he enters Hell.

* * *

The second of the matters which Allah, exalted is He, mentioned about the condition of this disbeliever is His saying: ﴿and he will be given to drink of festering water⁠﻿⁠ ﴿He will gulp it down but will hardly swallow it⁠﻿⁠. And here there are questions:

The first question: upon what is ﴿and he will be given to drink⁠﻿⁠ conjoined?

The answer: it is conjoined to an omitted element whose estimated meaning is: ﴿Ahead of him is Hell⁠﻿⁠, in which he will be cast, ﴿and he will be given to drink of festering water⁠﻿⁠.

The second question: the punishment of the people of the Fire has many aspects, so why was this state singled out for mention?

The answer: this state is likely among the most severe kinds of punishment, so it was singled out for mention together with His saying: ﴿and death will come to him from every place, yet he will not die.⁠﻿⁠

The third question: what is the meaning of ﴿of festering water⁠﻿⁠?

The answer: it is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān). The estimated meaning is: when He said ﴿he will be given to drink of water⁠﻿⁠, it was as if it were said: "And what is that water?" He said: ﴿festering⁠﻿⁠. And al-ṣadīd is what flows from the skins of the people of the Fire. It is also said that the estimated meaning is "he will be given to drink of water like festering matter," by Allah creating in Hell what resembles festering matter in stench, thickness, and filth, and it is also itself festering, because its repulsiveness prevents one from taking it. This is like His saying: ﴿And they are given drink of scalding water, which cuts their intestines﴾ [Muḥammad: 15], and ﴿And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal, which scalds the faces. Wretched is the drink﴾ [al-Kahf: 29].

The fourth question: what is the meaning of ﴿He will gulp it down but will hardly swallow it⁠﻿⁠?
