Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verse 21:

[Page 85]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will all come forth before God, and the weak will say to those who were arrogant, "Indeed, we were your followers, so can you avail us anything against the punishment of God?" They will say, "Had God guided us, we would have guided you. It is all the same for us whether we lament or endure patiently; there is no escape for us."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the kinds of punishment of these disbelievers, and then mentioned right after it that their deeds would become void and false, in this verse He mentioned the manner of their shame when their followers clung to them and the manner of their exposure before them. This is a reference to the spiritual punishment that results from disgrace and shame. There are several issues here:

The first issue: "baraza" (came forth) in the language means "appeared after being hidden." From it, the wide open space is called "al-barāz" because it is manifest. It was said regarding His saying, ﴿and you will see the earth bare﴾ [al-Kahf: 47], meaning apparent, with nothing covering it. A woman is called "barzah" if she appears before people. It is said: "So-and-so came forth above his peers" when he surpassed and outdid them, and its origin is in horses: when one of them outpaces the others, it is said: "It came forth over them," as if it emerged from their midst and became visible.

Having known this, we say: here there are discussions.

The first discussion: His saying, "And they came forth," is expressed in the past tense, though its meaning is future, because everything God, exalted is He, reports is true and real, so it is as if it has already occurred and entered existence. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of Paradise﴾ [al-A'raf: 50].

The second discussion: We have mentioned that "coming forth" in the language is an expression for appearing after concealment, and this is impossible with respect to God, exalted is He, so it necessarily requires interpretation. This has several aspects:

The first: They used to conceal themselves from eyes when committing indecencies, and they thought that this was hidden from God, exalted is He. So when the Day of Resurrection comes, they will be uncovered before God, exalted is He, in their own estimation, and they will know that nothing hidden is concealed from Him.

The second: They came out of their graves and thus came forth for God's reckoning and judgment.

The third, which is the interpretation of the philosophers: When the soul separates from the body, it is as if the covering and the cushion are removed, and it remains stripped in its own essence, bare of everything other than itself. That is what "coming forth to God" means.

The third discussion: Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: His saying, "And they came forth to God," is what is meant by His saying in the previous verse: ﴿and behind him is a harsh punishment﴾.

Know that His saying, "And they came forth to God," is close to His saying: ﴿On the Day when the secrets are tested, he will have no power and no helper﴾ [al-Tariq: 9-10]. That is because the inner states appear on that day and the hidden conditions are uncovered. If they are among the blessed, they will come forth before the Wise Judge with their holy attributes, their lofty states, their radiant faces, and their pure, illuminated spirits. Then the light of majesty will be revealed to them, and the radiance of the world of holiness will greatly shine upon them. How exalted those states are! But if they are among the wretched, they will come forth to the place of greatness and the stations of pride, humiliated, degraded, submissive, humbled, and falling into the disgrace of shame, the abasement of exposure, and the position of contempt and terror. We seek refuge in God from that.

Then God, exalted is He, related that the weak will say to the leaders: "Can you ward off God's punishment from us?" The meaning is: We only followed you for this day. Then the leaders will acknowledge their disgrace, impotence, and humiliation, and they will say: ﴿It is all the same for us whether we lament or endure patiently; there is no escape for us.﴾ It is known that the acknowledgment by the leaders, chiefs, and those who were followed of such impotence, disgrace, and calamity necessitates great shame and complete, total humiliation. So the purpose of mentioning this verse is the seizure of the punishment of exposure, shame, and disgrace upon them, together with what was previously mentioned of the other aspects of the kinds of torment and punishment. We seek refuge in God from them. And God knows best.

[Page 86]

The second issue: In some copies of the Qur'an, "al-Du'afā'" (the weak) is written with a waw before the hamza. The reason for this is that it was written according to the pronunciation of those who emphasize the alif before the hamza, inclining it toward the waw. A parallel to this is "ʿulamāʾu Banī Isrāʾīl" (the scholars of the Children of Israel).

The third issue: "al-Du'afā'" are the followers and the common people, and "alladhīna istakbarū" (those who were arrogant) are the leaders and the great ones. Ibn ʿAbbās said: What is meant is their elders who were arrogant toward worshipping God, exalted is He. ﴿Indeed, we were your followers﴾, i.e., in the world. Al-Farrāʾ and most of the lexicographers said: "Tabaʿ" is a singular noun like "khādim" and "khadam," "bāqir" and "baqar," "ḥāris" and "ḥaras," "rāṣid" and "raṣad." Al-Zajjāj said: It is also permissible that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as a name, meaning "we were possessors of following."

Know that this following may be understood as following in disbelief, and it may be that what is meant by it is following in the affairs of this world. ﴿So can you avail us anything against the punishment of God?﴾ i.e., can you ward off God's punishment from us?

If it is asked: What is the difference between "min" in His saying ﴿min ʿadhābi Llāh﴾ (against the punishment of God) and "min" in His saying ﴿min shayʾ﴾ (anything)?

We say: Both are for partitive meaning, as if to say: Can you avail us some part of something that is God's punishment? That is, some part of God's punishment. At this point, God, exalted is He, related about those who were arrogant that they said: ﴿Had God guided us, we would have guided you,﴾ and in this there are several aspects:

The first: Ibn ʿAbbās said: Its meaning is, "Had God guided us, we would have guided you." al-Wāḥidī said: Its meaning is that they only called them to misguidance, because God had misguided them and did not guide them; so they called their followers to misguidance. Had He guided them, they would have called them to guidance. The author of al-Kashshāf said: Perhaps they said this while lying in it, and this is indicated by His saying, exalted is He, quoting the hypocrites: ﴿On the Day God resurrects them all, they will swear to Him just as they swear to you﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 18].

Know that the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) do not permit the occurrence of lies from the people of the Resurrection, so this statement from them contradicts the principles of their teachers and is not accepted from them.

The second: The author of al-Kashshāf said: It is possible that the meaning is: Had we been among the people of lutf (divine grace, kindness that facilitates obedience), and our Lord had shown us grace so that we were guided, we would have guided you to faith. al-Qadi (ʿAbd al-Jabbār) mentioned this aspect and refuted it, saying: It is not permissible to interpret this as lutf, because that has already been done by God, exalted is He.

The third: The meaning may be: Had God freed us from punishment and guided us to the path of Paradise, we would have guided you. The evidence that what is meant by guidance is this meaning that we have mentioned is that this is what they sought and requested, so it is necessary that the intended meaning of guidance be this sense.

Then He said: ﴿It is all the same for us whether we lament or endure patiently﴾, i.e., lamenting and enduring are equal for us. The hamza and "am" are for equalization. A parallel to this is: ﴿So endure patiently or do not; it is all the same for you﴾ [al-Tur: 16]. Then He said: ﴿There is no escape for us﴾, i.e., no refuge or place of flight. The word "maḥīṣ" may be a verbal noun like "maghīb" and "mashīb," and a place like "mabīt" and "madīq." It is said: "ḥāṣa ʿanhu" and "ḥāḍa ʿanhu" with one meaning. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verse 22 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided: Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I betrayed you. And I had no authority over you, except that I invited you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me. Indeed, I disbelieved in what you associated [with Allah] before. Indeed, for the wrongdoers is a painful punishment.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, mentioned the debate that took place between the leaders and the followers among the disbelievers of mankind, He followed it with the debate that took place between Satan and his followers among mankind. So He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided.﴾ Regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿when the matter has been decided﴾, there are several views.

The first view: The exegetes said: When the people of Paradise have settled in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire, the people of the Fire begin to blame Iblis (Iblis, the name of the chief of the devils) and rebuke him. He stands among them in the Fire as an orator and says what Allah has reported of him with His saying: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided.﴾

The second view: that what is meant by His saying ﴿the matter has been decided﴾ is when the reckoning has ended. The first view is preferable, because the final state of the people of the Resurrection is the settling of the obedient in Paradise and the settling of the disbelievers in the Fire, and then the matter continues after that.

The third view, which is our school's position, is that the sinful among the People of the Prayer will come out of the Fire and enter Paradise. So it is not far-fetched that what is meant by His saying ﴿when the matter has been decided﴾ is that time, because at that time the considered states come to an end, and nothing comes after it except the continuation of what occurred before it. As for "Satan," what is meant is Iblis, because the word "Satan" is singular and so applies to one individual, and Iblis is the head and chief of the devils. So interpreting the word as referring to him is preferable, especially since the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah gathers the creation and judges between them, the disbeliever will say: The Muslims have found someone to intercede for them, so who will intercede for us? It is none but Iblis who misled us. So they will come to him and ask him, and at that point he will say this statement."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I betrayed you﴾, there are several discussions:

The first discussion: The meaning is that Allah, may He be exalted, promised you the promise of truth, which is resurrection and recompense for deeds, and He fulfilled for you what He promised you. I promised you the opposite of that, but I betrayed you. The explanation of the statement is that the soul inclines toward these worldly conditions and cannot conceive the nature of the otherworldly felicities and the spiritual perfections, while Allah calls to them and encourages them, as He said: ﴿But the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ [al-A'la: 17].

The second discussion: His saying ﴿the promise of truth﴾ is of the type of attributing a thing to itself, like His saying ﴿and the grain of the harvest﴾ and "the Friday mosque" according to the Kufans. The meaning is: He promised you the true promise. According to the Basrans, the implied phrase is: the promise of the true day, or the true matter; or the implied phrase is: He promised you the truth. Then He mentioned the verbal noun for emphasis.

The third discussion: There is an ellipsis in the verse in two respects:

The first: The implied sense is: Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and He fulfilled it, and I promised you, but I betrayed you. This was omitted because that situation indicates the truthfulness of that promise, since they were witnessing it, and there is no explanation beyond direct sight. Also, because He mentioned the breaking of promise in the case of Satan's promise, this indicates the truthfulness of Allah's promise, may He be exalted.

The second: In His saying ﴿and I promised you, but I betrayed you﴾, the verb "promised" requires a second object, which is omitted here because it is known. The implied sense is: I promised you that there is no Paradise, no Fire, no gathering, and no reckoning.

Page 88

As for His saying ﴿And I had no authority over you﴾, that is, no power, capacity, domination, or compulsion, by which I could force you into disbelief and sins and compel you to them. ﴿Except that I invited you﴾, that is, except my calling you to misguidance through my whispering and my adornment. The grammarians said: invitation is not of the same kind as authority, so His saying ﴿except that I invited you﴾ is like the saying of people: "Their greeting is nothing but beating." Al-Wahidi said: it is a disjunctive exception, meaning "but I invited you." In my view, it is possible to say that the word "except" here is a genuine exception, because a person's ability to move another to an action is sometimes by compulsion and force, and sometimes by strengthening the motive in his heart by casting whisperings into it. This latter is a kind of domination. Moreover, the apparent meaning of this verse indicates that Satan has no power to strike a person down, to twist his limbs and organs, or to remove his intellect, as the common people and the Hashwiyya claim. Then He said: ﴿So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾, meaning: what came from me was only calling and whispering, and you had heard the proofs of Allah and witnessed the coming of the prophets of Allah, so it was obligatory upon you not to be deceived by my words nor to pay heed to me. When you preferred my word over the clear proofs, the blame lies upon you and not upon me in this matter. There are two issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: The Mu'tazilah said: this verse indicates several things:

First: If disbelief and disobedience came from Allah, it would be necessary to say: "So do not blame me, nor yourselves, for Allah decreed disbelief upon you and compelled you to it."

Second: The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that Satan has no power to strike a person down, to twist his limbs, or to remove the intellect from him, as the Hashwiyya and the common people say.

Third: This verse indicates that a person may not be blamed, reproached, or punished for the act of another. At this point it becomes clear that it is not permissible to punish the children of disbelievers for the disbelief of their fathers.

Some of our companions answered these points: that this is the statement of Satan, so it is not permissible to rely on it.

The opponent replied: if this statement were false, Allah would have clarified its falsehood and made its rejection manifest. Moreover, there is no benefit on that day in mentioning this false speech and corrupt statement. Do you not see that His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I betrayed you﴾ is a true statement, and His saying ﴿And I had no authority over you﴾ is a true statement, as evidenced by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the misguided﴾ [al-Hijr: 42].

* * *

The second issue: This verse indicates that the primary Satan is the self (nafs), because Satan made clear that he came only with whispering. Were it not for the inclination produced by desire, anger, illusion, and imagination, his whispering would have had no effect at all. This shows that the primary Satan is the self.

If someone asks: explain to us the reality of whispering.

We say: An act proceeds from a person only when four matters occur, each following the other with necessary natural order. Its explanation: the organs of a person, by their original soundness and natural fitness, are capable of doing and refraining, of advancing and withdrawing. So as long as no inclination arises in the heart toward preferring the act over its omission or the reverse, the act cannot proceed. That inclination is the decisive will and the decisive intention. Then that decisive will arises only when there is knowledge, belief, or conjecture that the act is a cause of benefit or a cause of harm. If this belief does not arise, no inclination arises either toward the act or toward its omission. The sum is that when a person perceives something, there follows his awareness that it is agreeable to him, or repugnant to him, or neither agreeable nor repugnant. If he becomes aware that it is agreeable, the decisive inclination toward the act follows. If he becomes aware that it is repugnant, the decisive inclination toward abstention follows. If neither, no inclination arises either toward that thing or toward its opposite, and the person remains as he was. When that decisive inclination arises, power together with that inclination becomes necessitating of the act.

Having understood this, we say: the proceeding of the act from the combination of the existing power and motive is something necessary, so Satan has no part in it. The proceeding of the inclination from the conception of it as good or the conception of it as evil is necessary, so Satan has no part in it. The arising of the conception of its being good or its being evil from the bare awareness of its essence is a necessary matter, so Satan has no part in it. Thus Satan has no part in any of these stages except in bringing something to mind, by casting his discourse into it, such as when a person was heedless of the image of a woman and Satan casts her description into his thought. Satan has no power except in this stage, and this is exactly what Allah reported of him when he said: ﴿And I had no authority over you, except that I invited you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me.﴾ That is, what came from me was nothing but this mere calling. As for the remaining stages, they did not proceed from me, and I had no effect whatsoever upon them.

* * *

Two questions remain at this point:

The first question: How is it conceivable that Satan can penetrate the inside of a person's organs and cast whispering into him?

The answer: People hold two views concerning angels and devils:

The first view: Everything other than Allah, by rational division, falls into three categories: that which occupies space, that which inheres in what occupies space, and that which neither occupies space nor inheres in it. Proof has never been established for the invalidity of the view concerning this third category; rather, numerous proofs have been established for its validity. This is what is called "spirits." If these spirits are pure, sacred, from the realm of holy spiritual beings, they are the angels; and if they are wicked, calling to evils and dwelling in the realm of bodies and abodes of darkness, they are the devils.

Having understood this, we say: on this assumption, Satan is not a body that needs to enter into the interior of the body, but is a spiritual substance of wicked action, inclined to evil. The human self is likewise. So on this assumption it is not far-fetched that some of those spirits cast various kinds of whisperings and falsehoods into the essence of the human self.

Some scholars mentioned in this matter a second possibility: that human rational souls differ in kind, forming groups, and each group is in charge of one particular spirit of the heavenly spirits. One type of human soul is of good character, noble conduct, characterized by joy, cheerfulness, and ease of affairs, and it is connected to a specific heavenly spirit. Another group is characterized by sharpness, force, harshness, and indifference to matters, and it is connected to another heavenly spirit. These human spirits are like children to that heavenly spirit, like its results and like branches sprouting from it. That heavenly spirit is the one that undertakes guiding them to their interests, and it is the one that grants them inspirations in both sleep and waking. The ancients called that heavenly spirit the "complete nature." There is no doubt that this heavenly spirit, which is the origin and fountain, has many branches and many results, all of which are of the same kind as this human spirit; and because of their similarity and kinship, some of them help one another in works suited to them and acts appropriate to their natures. Then, if they are good, pure, and virtuous, they are angels, and that aid is called inspiration. And if they are

Page 90

[Page 91]

…evil, wicked, and ugly in its deeds, were devils. And that assistance was called whispering (waswasa). Some scholars also mentioned a third possibility regarding this. It is that human souls and human spirits, when they separate from their bodies, grow strong in those qualities they acquired in those bodies and become perfected in them. When another soul arises that resembles that separated soul, in a body resembling the body of that separated soul, a kind of attachment occurs between that separated soul and this body, because of the resemblance between this body and what had been the body of that separated soul. The separated soul thus becomes strongly attached to this body, and that separated soul becomes a helper to this soul attached to this body, and a supporter of it in its actions and states, because of this resemblance. Then, if this meaning concerns matters of goodness and blessings, it is inspiration (ilham), and if it concerns evil, it is whispering (waswasa). These are possible interpretations, derived from the view that there exist holy substances (jawahir qudsiyya) free from corporeality and spatiality. The view that there are pure and impure spirits is a well-known doctrine among the early philosophers, so they have no right to deny that it is attributed to the Lawgiver of our religion, Muhammad (ﷺ).

As for the second view, namely that angels and devils must be bodies, we say: on this assumption it is impossible to say that they are dense bodies. Rather, it must be said that they are subtle bodies, and God, glory be to Him, composed them in a wondrous composition, such that despite their subtlety they do not accept dispersal, disintegration, corruption, or annihilation. The penetration of subtle bodies into the depths of dense bodies is not far-fetched. Do you not see that the human spirit is a subtle body, and that it penetrates into the inner depths of the body? If this is understood, how can the penetration of many kinds of subtle bodies into the inside of this body be deemed far-fetched? Does not the substance of fire permeate the substance of charcoal, rose water permeate rose petals, and sesame oil flow through the body of sesame? So it is here as well. From what we have established it becomes clear that the affirmation of jinn and devils is a matter that reason does not reject and that evidence does not refute, and that persistence in denial is nothing but a result of ignorance and lack of discernment. Since it has been established that the view of the existence of devils is possible in general, we say: the more correct and preferable position is that the angels, according to this view, are created from light, and the devils are created from smoke and flame, as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of the scorching wind﴾ [al-Hijr: 27]. This statement is among the well-known views of the early philosophers, so how is it fitting for a sensible person to find it far-fetched from the Lawgiver of our religion, Muhammad (ﷺ)?

The second question: Why did Satan say: ﴿So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾, while he himself is also blameworthy for undertaking that false whispering?

The answer: He meant by this, "Do not blame me for what you did, but blame yourselves for it, because you deviated from what the guidance of God, Exalted is He, requires of you." Then God, Exalted is He, said, relating from Satan that he said: ﴿I cannot help you, nor can you help me﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: Ibn Abbas said: "I cannot relieve you or rescue you." Ibn al-A'rabi said: "The one who cries out (al-sarikh) is the one who seeks help, and the one who answers (al-musrikh) is the one who gives help. It is said: 'So-and-so cried out (sarakha) when he sought help, and said: "O, help me!" (wa-ghawthah), and I answered him (asrakhtuhu), meaning I helped him."

The second issue: Hamzah recited "bi-musrikhiyya" with a kasra on the ya'. Al-Wahidi said: this is the reading of al-A'mash and Yahya ibn Wathhab. Al-Farra' said: "It is probably an error of the readers, for few of them are free from error. He probably thought that the ba' in His words ﴿bi-musrikhiyya﴾ governs the whole word, and this is an error, because the ya' is the ya' of the first person and is excluded from that." He said: "What we see as an error in it is His words ﴿We shall leave him to what he has turned to, and burn him in Hell﴾ [al-Nisa': 115], with the jazm on the ha'. They thought, God knows best, that the jazm is on the ha', and this is an error, because the ha' is in the position of an accusative (nasb), and the verb before it has been put in the jussive (jazm) by the dropping of the ya' from it. Some grammarians went to great lengths to mention an explanation for its validity, but most of them said that it is a grammatical error (lahn). God knows best."

Then God, Exalted is He, said, relating from him: ﴿Indeed, I disbelieved in what you associated with me before﴾. In this there are several issues:

The first issue: The "ma" in His words ﴿Indeed, I disbelieved in what you associated with me before﴾ has two views:

The first: it is a verbal-noun (masdariyya) particle, and the meaning is: "I disbelieved in your associating me with God, Exalted is He, in obedience." The meaning is that he denied what those followers believed, namely that Iblis is a partner of God, Exalted is He, in governing this world, and he disbelieved in that. Or the meaning may be that they used to obey Satan in deeds of evil just as they used to obey God in deeds of good, and this is what is meant by association (ishrak).

The second, which is the view of al-Farra': the meaning is that Iblis said, "I disbelieved in God, in whom you associated me before your disbelief," meaning that his disbelief preceded the disbelief of those followers. In this case the "ma" in this place means "man" (who). The first view is correct, because the speech is coherent only with the first explanation. It is also possible to say that the speech is coherent with the second explanation, and the sense is as if he said: "My whispering had no effect on your disbelief, as is shown by the fact that I disbelieved before you fell into disbelief. My disbelief was not caused by another whispering, otherwise an infinite regress would follow. Thus it is established that the cause of falling into disbelief is something other than whispering." On this assumption the speech is coherent.

As for His words ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will have a painful punishment﴾, the more apparent view is that it is the speech of God, Mighty and Majestic, and that Iblis's speech ended before this statement. It is also not far-fetched that this is part of Iblis's remaining speech, cutting off the hopes of those disbelievers for assistance and help. God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verse 23:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be admitted to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein by the permission of their Lord; their greeting therein will be, "Peace."﴾

And concerning it there are two issues:

The first issue: Know that when He, may He be exalted, had elaborated at length on the states of the wretched from many aspects, He then explained the states of the blessed. You have already learned that reward must be a pure, lasting benefit joined with honor. The pure benefit is indicated by His saying: ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be admitted to gardens beneath which rivers flow.﴾ Its being lasting is indicated by His saying: ﴿abiding therein.﴾ The honor arises from two aspects:

The first: that those benefits came about by the permission and command of Allah, may He be exalted.

The second: His saying: ﴿their greeting therein will be, "Peace."﴾ For some of them greet one another with this word, and the angels greet them with it, as He said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, [saying], "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23-24]. And the Lord, the Merciful, also greets them with this word, as He said: ﴿"Peace," a word from a Lord, Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58].

Know that "al-Salam" (peace) is derived from "al-Salamah" (safety); otherwise it would be apparent that the meaning is that they were safe from the afflictions and regrets of this world, or from the various kinds of its pains and diseases, and the varieties of its griefs and anxieties. How true is what they said, for safety from the trials of the world of bodies, which is corrupt and perishable, is among the greatest of blessings, especially when, after deliverance from it, one attains the joy of the spirit and the angelic happiness.

The second issue: al-Hasan recited: "wa-Udkhilu alladhina amanu" (and I will admit those who believed), with the meaning "and I will admit them," and according to this recitation, His saying ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾ is connected to what follows it, i.e., "their greeting therein will be peace by the permission of their Lord." That is: the angels greet them by the permission of their Lord.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verses 24–26 (part 1 of 2):**

God's words: ﴿Have you not considered how God sets forth a parable: a good word is like a good tree, its root firm and its branches in the sky? It yields its fruit every season by the permission of its Lord. God sets forth parables for people, that they may take heed.﴾ ﴿And the likeness of an evil word is like an evil tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability.﴾

Know that when God explained the conditions of the wretched and the conditions of the blessed, He presented an example that clarifies the state of these two groups in their judgment, and this is the parable. In it there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Know that God mentioned a tree described by four attributes, and then likened the good word to it.

The first attribute of that tree is that it is good (*ṭayyiba*), and this may carry several meanings:

First, that it is good in its appearance, form and shape.
Second, that it is good in its fragrance.
Third, that it is good in its fruit, meaning that the fruits produced from it are delicious and pleasant.
Fourth, that it is good in respect of its benefit, meaning that just as its eating is enjoyable, so its benefit is great. The phrase "a good tree" must be understood as encompassing all of these aspects, for their combination produces perfect goodness.

The second attribute is His words: ﴿its root is firm﴾, meaning established, enduring, secure against being uprooted, cut off, removed or perished. This is because a good thing that is on the verge of disappearance and ending brings joy at finding it, yet great sorrow arises from fear of its loss and end. But when it is known of its state that it is lasting and permanent, not vanishing or ending, then the joy of finding it grows greater and the delight of gaining it becomes complete.

The third attribute is His words: ﴿and its branches are in the sky﴾. This description indicates the perfection of that tree's condition in two respects:
First, that the rising of the branches and their strength in ascending indicates the firmness of the root and the solidity of the roots.
Second, that when it rises high, it is far from the decay of the earth and the filth of buildings, so its fruits are pure, clean and free from all impurities.

The fourth attribute is His words: ﴿it yields its fruit every season by the permission of its Lord﴾. The meaning is that the tree described has this quality: its fruit is always present, at all times, and it is not like trees whose fruit is present only at some times and not others. This is the explanation of the tree that God mentioned in this noble Book. And it is known by necessity that the desire to attain such a tree must be great, and that the rational person, when able to obtain and possess it, must not neglect it or be negligent in winning it.

Having understood this, we say: the knowledge of God (*ma'rifat Allah*), and being utterly absorbed in His love, His service and His obedience, resembles this tree in these four attributes.

As for the first attribute, which is its goodness, it is present. Indeed we say: there is in reality no good or pleasure except this knowledge. This is because the pleasure obtained from eating a particular fruit arises from the fact that the perception of that fruit is agreeable to the temperament of the body; and because of that agreement and suitability, that great pleasure is produced. Here, what is agreeable to the essence of the rational soul (*al-nafs al-nutqiyya*) and the holy spirit (*al-ruh al-qudsiyya*) is nothing but the knowledge of God, His love, and being utterly absorbed in delight in Him. Therefore this knowledge must be extremely delightful. Indeed we say: the pleasure arising from the perception of fruit must be of lesser state than the pleasure arising from the illumination of the essence of the soul through the knowledge of God. The explanation of this difference is in several respects:

The first respect: sensible objects become perceived only because the surface of the sense organ meets the surface of the object perceived. As for the claim that the substance of the sensed object penetrates into the substance of the sense organ, this is not so, because bodies cannot interpenetrate. But here, the knowledge of God, that light and that illumination, becomes flowing within the substance of the soul, united with it, and as if the soul, at the arrival of that illumination, becomes other than the soul that was before the arrival of that illumination. Thus this is a great difference between the two domains.

The second respect of difference: in the delight of fruit, the perceiving faculty is the faculty of taste, and the perceived is the particular flavor. Here, the perceiver is the essence of the holy soul, and the known and the object of awareness is the very Essence of the Truth, may His majesty be exalted, and the attributes of His majesty and generosity. Therefore the relation between one of the two pleasures to the other must be like the relation between one of the two objects of perception to the other.

The third respect of difference: the pleasures obtained from eating good fruit, whenever they are obtained, pass away immediately, because they are a quality that quickly changes and is very subject to alteration. But the perfection and majesty of the Truth cannot be subject to change or transformation, and the readiness of the substance of the soul to receive that happiness is also incapable of change. Thus the great difference appears from this respect.

Know that the difference between the two kinds may be nearly of infinite respects, so these three respects suffice, as a reminder to the sound intellect regarding the rest.

As for the second attribute, namely that this tree has a firm root, this attribute is stronger and more perfect in the tree of the knowledge of God. This is because the roots of this tree are firmly fixed in the substance of the holy soul, and this substance is a pure essence, free from coming-into-being and corruption, far from change and perishing. Moreover, the sustenance of this firmness comes from the manifestation of God's majesty, and this manifestation is a necessary consequence of His, glorified be He, being in His essence the Light of Lights and the Source of manifestation. This is something whose cessation is impossible by reason, because He, glorified be He, is necessarily existent by His essence, and what is necessarily existent is so in all its attributes, while change, perishing, alteration, cessation, miserliness and withholding are impossible with respect to Him. Thus it is established that the tree described as having a firm root is none other than this tree.

**The third attribute of this tree:** that its branches are such that they are in the sky.

Know that the tree of knowledge has branches rising into the air of the divine world, and branches rising into the air of the corporeal world.

As for the first kind: these are many categories, and what gathers them is his, upon him be peace, saying: "Reverence for the command of God" (*al-ta'zim li-amr Allah*). This includes reflection upon the signs of the knowledge of God, the Exalted, in the world of spirits, in the world of bodies, in the conditions of the world of spheres and stars, and in the conditions of the lower world. It also includes: love of God, the Exalted, longing for God, the Exalted, persistence in the remembrance of God, the Exalted, complete reliance upon God, the Exalted, and complete severance from all other than God, the Exalted. To enumerate these categories in detail is not something to hope for, because these states are endless.

As for the second kind: these are many categories, and what gathers them is his, upon him be peace, saying: "Compassion for the creatures of God" (*al-shafaqa 'ala khalq Allah*). This includes mercy, tenderness, forgiveness, overlooking sins, striving to bring good to them, averting evil from them, and repaying evil with good. These categories too are endless, and they are firm branches of the tree of the knowledge of God. For the more a person penetrates deeply into the knowledge of God, the more perfect, stronger and more excellent these states become for him.

**The fourth attribute:** His words, the Exalted: ﴿it yields its fruit every season by the permission of its Lord﴾. This tree is more worthy of this attribute than corporeal trees, because the tree of knowledge necessitates these states and is effective in bringing them about, and the cause does not separate from its effect. Thus the effect of the firm rooting of the tree of knowledge in the soil of the heart is that its sight becomes by way of reflection, as He said: ﴿So take warning, O you with eyes﴾ [al-Hashr 59:2]; and that its hearing becomes by way of wisdom, as He said: ﴿who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾ [al-Zumar 39:18]; and that its speech becomes truthful and right, as He said: ﴿Be steadfast in justice, witnesses for God, even if it be against yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa 4:135], and he, upon him be peace, said: "Speak the truth even if it be against yourselves." And this person, the more firm the tree of knowledge is in the soil of his heart, the stronger and more perfect it is, and the more these effects appear in him. Perhaps he goes so deeply into this matter that whatever he observes, he observes the Truth in it; and perhaps his advancement in it becomes so great that he sees nothing without having already seen God before it. This is what is meant by His words, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿it yields its fruit every season by the permission of its Lord﴾.

Moreover, what we have mentioned is an indication of the psychic inspirations and the spiritual dispositions that arise in the substances of the spirits. Then there continually ascends from them, at every season, moment and glance, good speech, righteous deed, humility, submission, weeping and lowliness, like the fruit of this tree.

As for His words: ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾, there is in it a wondrous subtlety. This is because at the attainment of these lofty states and exalted ranks, a person may rejoice in them for what they are in themselves, and he may ascend further so that he no longer rejoices in them for what they are in themselves, but rejoices in them only because they come from the Master (*al-mawla*). At that point his joy is in reality in the Master, not in these states. For this reason one of the realized scholars (*al-muhaqqiqin*) said: "Whoever prefers gnosis for the sake of gnosis has spoken of the transient; and whoever prefers gnosis not for the sake of gnosis, but for the sake of the Known (*al-ma'ruf*), has plunged into the depths of arrival." Thus it has become clear, by this exposition we have explained and this clarification we have detailed, that this parable which God mentioned in this Book is a parable guiding to the world of holiness, the presence of majesty, and the pavilions of greatness. So we ask God, the Exalted, for increased guidance and mercy; indeed He is All-Hearing, All-Responsive.

Some of them have also stated, in explaining this parable, a statement that is not objectionable. He said: God, glorified and exalted be He, likened faith to a tree, because a tree does not deserve to be called a tree except by three things: a firm root, a standing trunk, and high branches. Likewise, faith is not complete except by three things: knowledge in the heart, speech with the tongue, and action with the body. And God knows best.

**The second issue:** The author of the *Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) said: concerning the accusative case in His words ﴿a good word﴾ (*kalima tayyiba*), there are two possibilities:

The first: it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, and the estimated meaning is: "He made a good word like a good tree," and this is an explanation of His words ﴿God set forth a parable﴾ (*darab Allah mathalan*).

The second: he said, "It is also permissible that *mathalan* (a parable) be in the accusative and *kalima* (word) be governed by *daraba* (set forth), meaning: He set forth a good word as a parable, in the sense of making it a parable." And His words ﴿like a good tree﴾ are the predicate of an omitted subject, and the estimated meaning is: "It is like a good tree."

The third: the author of *Hall al-'Aqd* said: "I think the more correct view is that His words ﴿kalima﴾ be treated as an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*), and the particle *ka* (like) in His words ﴿like a tree﴾ is in the place of the accusative, in the sense of 'the likeness of a good tree'."

**The third issue:** Ibn 'Abbas said: the good word is the saying "There is no god but God" (*la ilaha illa Allah*), and the good tree is the date palm, according to the majority. The author of the *Kashshaf* said: it is every fruit-bearing tree with good fruit, such as the date palm, the fig tree, the grapevine and the pomegranate; and by "good tree" he meant its fruit, but he did not mention it because the context points to it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verses 24–26 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Its root is firm﴾, meaning the root of this good tree is firmly established. ﴿And its branches are in the sky﴾, meaning its highest part is in the sky, and what is meant by the sky is the air, because everything that is above you and raises you up is called a sky. ﴿It yields its fruit﴾, meaning this tree gives ﴿its produce﴾, that is, its dates and whatever is eaten from it, ﴿every season﴾. The scholars differed over the interpretation of this "season" (hin). Ibn 'Abbas said it is six months, because the period between its bearing and its harvesting is six months. A man came to Ibn 'Abbas and said: "I vowed not to speak to my brother for a hin," and he said: "The hin is six months," and he recited His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It yields its produce every season﴾. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said it is a year, because the tree bears fruit from one year to the next. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said it is two months, because the period in which a palm tree is fed is two months. Al-Zajjaj said: "All of the people of the language (Ahl al-Lughah, the scholars of Arabic lexicography) whom we have encountered hold that hin is a noun like 'time' (waqt), which applies to all periods of time, whether long or short. What is meant by His saying ﴿It yields its produce every season﴾ is that one benefits from it at every time and every hour, by night or by day, in winter or in summer." They said: "The reason is that when people leave the dates on the palm from one year to the next, they benefit from it throughout all the seasons of the year."

I say: Although these scholars were correct in their investigation of the individual words of the verse, they strayed from grasping the intended meaning. This is because He, exalted is He, described this tree with the attributes mentioned, and there is no need for us to determine whether that tree is the palm or something else. We know by necessity that the tree described with these four mentioned attributes is a noble tree, and every intelligent person should strive to obtain it and make it his own, whether or not it exists in this world, because this attribute is something that is to be sought. Their disagreement over the interpretation of hin is also of this kind. And God knows best the matters.

Then He said: ﴿And God sets forth parables for the people, that perhaps they may remember﴾. The meaning is that in setting forth parables there is an increase in understanding, reminding, and depicting meanings. This is because purely intellectual meanings are not received by the senses, the imagination, or the faculty of estimation (wahm). So when something similar to them from among sensible things is mentioned, the senses, the imagination, and the faculty of estimation abandon that resistance, the intelligible is fitted onto the sensible, and complete understanding and arrival at the desired goal are attained through it.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the likeness of a corrupt word is that of a corrupt tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability﴾.

Know that the corrupt tree is ignorance of God, for it is the first of calamities, the title of disobedience, and the head of wretchedness. Then He, exalted is He, likened it to a tree described with three attributes:

The first attribute: it is corrupt. Some said it is garlic, because the Prophet (ﷺ) described garlic as a corrupt tree. [p. 96]
It was also said it is leek (al-kurrath). It was said it is the colocynth tree (al-hanzal), because of the many harms in it. It was said it is the thorn tree.

Know that this detailed specification is unnecessary, for a tree may be corrupt in terms of its smell, may be corrupt in terms of its taste, may be corrupt in terms of its form and appearance, and may be corrupt in terms of containing many harms. The tree that combines all these attributes, even if it does not exist, is nonetheless one whose attributes are known, so likening to it is beneficial for the intended goal.

The second attribute: His saying ﴿uprooted from the surface of the earth﴾. This attribute corresponds to His saying ﴿its root is firm﴾. The meaning of ijtuththat is "it was uprooted," and the real meaning of ijtithath is taking the whole body. His saying ﴿from the surface of the earth﴾ means that it has no root and no stem. Likewise, associating partners with God, exalted is He, has no proof, no stability, and no strength.

The third attribute: His saying ﴿having no stability﴾. This attribute is like a complement to the second attribute. The meaning is that it has no permanence. It is said: "The thing settled (qarra) a settling (qarar)," like your saying: "It remained firm, a firmness (thabat)." It likened to it the statement that is not supported by proof, which is therefore rejected and not established.

Know that this example describing the corrupt word is at the utmost perfection, because He, exalted is He, clarified that it is described as having many harms and is devoid of all benefits. As for it being described with harms, the reference to this is in His saying ﴿corrupt﴾, and as for it being devoid of all benefits, the reference to this is in His saying ﴿uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability﴾. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verses 24–26 (part 1 of 2):**

God's words: ﴿Have you not considered how God sets forth a parable: a good word is like a good tree, its root firm and its branches in the sky? It yields its fruit every season by the permission of its Lord. God sets forth parables for people, that they may take heed.﴾ ﴿And the likeness of an evil word is like an evil tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability.﴾

Know that when God explained the conditions of the wretched and the conditions of the blessed, He presented an example that clarifies the state of these two groups in their judgment, and this is the parable. In it there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Know that God mentioned a tree described by four attributes, and then likened the good word to it.

The first attribute of that tree is that it is good (*ṭayyiba*), and this may carry several meanings:

First, that it is good in its appearance, form and shape.
Second, that it is good in its fragrance.
Third, that it is good in its fruit, meaning that the fruits produced from it are delicious and pleasant.
Fourth, that it is good in respect of its benefit, meaning that just as its eating is enjoyable, so its benefit is great. The phrase "a good tree" must be understood as encompassing all of these aspects, for their combination produces perfect goodness.

The second attribute is His words: ﴿its root is firm﴾, meaning established, enduring, secure against being uprooted, cut off, removed or perished. This is because a good thing that is on the verge of disappearance and ending brings joy at finding it, yet great sorrow arises from fear of its loss and end. But when it is known of its state that it is lasting and permanent, not vanishing or ending, then the joy of finding it grows greater and the delight of gaining it becomes complete.

The third attribute is His words: ﴿and its branches are in the sky﴾. This description indicates the perfection of that tree's condition in two respects:
First, that the rising of the branches and their strength in ascending indicates the firmness of the root and the solidity of the roots.
Second, that when it rises high, it is far from the decay of the earth and the filth of buildings, so its fruits are pure, clean and free from all impurities.

The fourth attribute is His words: ﴿it yields its fruit every season by the permission of its Lord﴾. The meaning is that the tree described has this quality: its fruit is always present, at all times, and it is not like trees whose fruit is present only at some times and not others. This is the explanation of the tree that God mentioned in this noble Book. And it is known by necessity that the desire to attain such a tree must be great, and that the rational person, when able to obtain and possess it, must not neglect it or be negligent in winning it.

Having understood this, we say: the knowledge of God (*ma'rifat Allah*), and being utterly absorbed in His love, His service and His obedience, resembles this tree in these four attributes.

As for the first attribute, which is its goodness, it is present. Indeed we say: there is in reality no good or pleasure except this knowledge. This is because the pleasure obtained from eating a particular fruit arises from the fact that the perception of that fruit is agreeable to the temperament of the body; and because of that agreement and suitability, that great pleasure is produced. Here, what is agreeable to the essence of the rational soul (*al-nafs al-nutqiyya*) and the holy spirit (*al-ruh al-qudsiyya*) is nothing but the knowledge of God, His love, and being utterly absorbed in delight in Him. Therefore this knowledge must be extremely delightful. Indeed we say: the pleasure arising from the perception of fruit must be of lesser state than the pleasure arising from the illumination of the essence of the soul through the knowledge of God. The explanation of this difference is in several respects:

The first respect: sensible objects become perceived only because the surface of the sense organ meets the surface of the object perceived. As for the claim that the substance of the sensed object penetrates into the substance of the sense organ, this is not so, because bodies cannot interpenetrate. But here, the knowledge of God, that light and that illumination, becomes flowing within the substance of the soul, united with it, and as if the soul, at the arrival of that illumination, becomes other than the soul that was before the arrival of that illumination. Thus this is a great difference between the two domains.

The second respect of difference: in the delight of fruit, the perceiving faculty is the faculty of taste, and the perceived is the particular flavor. Here, the perceiver is the essence of the holy soul, and the known and the object of awareness is the very Essence of the Truth, may His majesty be exalted, and the attributes of His majesty and generosity. Therefore the relation between one of the two pleasures to the other must be like the relation between one of the two objects of perception to the other.

The third respect of difference: the pleasures obtained from eating good fruit, whenever they are obtained, pass away immediately, because they are a quality that quickly changes and is very subject to alteration. But the perfection and majesty of the Truth cannot be subject to change or transformation, and the readiness of the substance of the soul to receive that happiness is also incapable of change. Thus the great difference appears from this respect.

Know that the difference between the two kinds may be nearly of infinite respects, so these three respects suffice, as a reminder to the sound intellect regarding the rest.

As for the second attribute, namely that this tree has a firm root, this attribute is stronger and more perfect in the tree of the knowledge of God. This is because the roots of this tree are firmly fixed in the substance of the holy soul, and this substance is a pure essence, free from coming-into-being and corruption, far from change and perishing. Moreover, the sustenance of this firmness comes from the manifestation of God's majesty, and this manifestation is a necessary consequence of His, glorified be He, being in His essence the Light of Lights and the Source of manifestation. This is something whose cessation is impossible by reason, because He, glorified be He, is necessarily existent by His essence, and what is necessarily existent is so in all its attributes, while change, perishing, alteration, cessation, miserliness and withholding are impossible with respect to Him. Thus it is established that the tree described as having a firm root is none other than this tree.

**The third attribute of this tree:** that its branches are such that they are in the sky.

Know that the tree of knowledge has branches rising into the air of the divine world, and branches rising into the air of the corporeal world.

As for the first kind: these are many categories, and what gathers them is his, upon him be peace, saying: "Reverence for the command of God" (*al-ta'zim li-amr Allah*). This includes reflection upon the signs of the knowledge of God, the Exalted, in the world of spirits, in the world of bodies, in the conditions of the world of spheres and stars, and in the conditions of the lower world. It also includes: love of God, the Exalted, longing for God, the Exalted, persistence in the remembrance of God, the Exalted, complete reliance upon God, the Exalted, and complete severance from all other than God, the Exalted. To enumerate these categories in detail is not something to hope for, because these states are endless.

As for the second kind: these are many categories, and what gathers them is his, upon him be peace, saying: "Compassion for the creatures of God" (*al-shafaqa 'ala khalq Allah*). This includes mercy, tenderness, forgiveness, overlooking sins, striving to bring good to them, averting evil from them, and repaying evil with good. These categories too are endless, and they are firm branches of the tree of the knowledge of God. For the more a person penetrates deeply into the knowledge of God, the more perfect, stronger and more excellent these states become for him.

This tree is more worthy of this attribute than corporeal trees, because the tree of knowledge necessitates these states and is effective in bringing them about, and the cause does not separate from its effect. And this person, the more firm the tree of knowledge is in the soil of his heart, the stronger and more perfect it is, and the more these effects appear in him. Perhaps he goes so deeply into this matter that whatever he observes, he observes the Truth in it; and perhaps his advancement in it becomes so great that he sees nothing without having already seen God before it. This is what is meant by His words, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿it yields its fruit every season by the permission of its Lord﴾.

Moreover, what we have mentioned is an indication of the psychic inspirations and the spiritual dispositions that arise in the substances of the spirits. Then there continually ascends from them, at every season, moment and glance, good speech, righteous deed, humility, submission, weeping and lowliness, like the fruit of this tree.

As for His words: ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾, there is in it a wondrous subtlety. This is because at the attainment of these lofty states and exalted ranks, a person may rejoice in them for what they are in themselves, and he may ascend further so that he no longer rejoices in them for what they are in themselves, but rejoices in them only because they come from the Master (*al-mawla*). At that point his joy is in reality in the Master, not in these states. For this reason one of the realized scholars (*al-muhaqqiqin*) said: "Whoever prefers gnosis for the sake of gnosis has spoken of the transient; and whoever prefers gnosis not for the sake of gnosis, but for the sake of the Known (*al-ma'ruf*), has plunged into the depths of arrival." Thus it has become clear, by this exposition we have explained and this clarification we have detailed, that this parable which God mentioned in this Book is a parable guiding to the world of holiness, the presence of majesty, and the pavilions of greatness. So we ask God, the Exalted, for increased guidance and mercy; indeed He is All-Hearing, All-Responsive.

Some of them have also stated, in explaining this parable, a statement that is not objectionable. He said: God, glorified and exalted be He, likened faith to a tree, because a tree does not deserve to be called a tree except by three things: a firm root, a standing trunk, and high branches. Likewise, faith is not complete except by three things: knowledge in the heart, speech with the tongue, and action with the body. And God knows best.

Then He said: ﴿And God sets forth parables for the people, that perhaps they may remember﴾. The meaning is that in setting forth parables there is an increase in understanding, reminding, and depicting meanings. This is because purely intellectual meanings are not received by the senses, the imagination, or the faculty of estimation (wahm). So when something similar to them from among sensible things is mentioned, the senses, the imagination, and the faculty of estimation abandon that resistance, the intelligible is fitted onto the sensible, and complete understanding and arrival at the desired goal are attained through it.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the likeness of a corrupt word is that of a corrupt tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability﴾.

Know that the corrupt tree is ignorance of God, for it is the first of calamities, the title of disobedience, and the head of wretchedness. Then He, exalted is He, likened it to a tree described with three attributes:

The first attribute: it is corrupt. Some said it is garlic, because the Prophet (ﷺ) described garlic as a corrupt tree. [p. 96]
It was also said it is leek (al-kurrath). It was said it is the colocynth tree (al-hanzal), because of the many harms in it. It was said it is the thorn tree.

Know that this detailed specification is unnecessary, for a tree may be corrupt in terms of its smell, may be corrupt in terms of its taste, may be corrupt in terms of its form and appearance, and may be corrupt in terms of containing many harms. The tree that combines all these attributes, even if it does not exist, is nonetheless one whose attributes are known, so likening to it is beneficial for the intended goal.

The meaning of ijtuththat is "it was uprooted," and the real meaning of ijtithath is taking the whole body. His saying ﴿from the surface of the earth﴾ means that it has no root and no stem. Likewise, associating partners with God, exalted is He, has no proof, no stability, and no strength.

The third attribute: His saying ﴿having no stability﴾. This attribute is like a complement to the second attribute. The meaning is that it has no permanence. It is said: "The thing settled (qarra) a settling (qarar)," like your saying: "It remained firm, a firmness (thabat)." It likened to it the statement that is not supported by proof, which is therefore rejected and not established.

Know that this example describing the corrupt word is at the utmost perfection, because He, exalted is He, clarified that it is described as having many harms and is devoid of all benefits. As for it being described with harms, the reference to this is in His saying ﴿corrupt﴾, and as for it being devoid of all benefits, the reference to this is in His saying ﴿uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability﴾. And God knows best.

We know by necessity that the tree described with these four mentioned attributes is a noble tree, and every intelligent person should strive to obtain it and make it his own, whether or not it exists in this world, because this attribute is something that is to be sought. Their disagreement over the interpretation of hin is also of this kind. And God knows best the matters.

Then He said: ﴿And God sets forth parables for the people, that perhaps they may remember﴾. The meaning is that in setting forth parables there is an increase in understanding, reminding, and depicting meanings. This is because purely intellectual meanings are not received by the senses, the imagination, or the faculty of estimation (wahm). So when something similar to them from among sensible things is mentioned, the senses, the imagination, and the faculty of estimation abandon that resistance, the intelligible is fitted onto the sensible, and complete understanding and arrival at the desired goal are attained through it.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the likeness of a corrupt word is that of a corrupt tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability﴾.

Know that the corrupt tree is ignorance of God, for it is the first of calamities, the title of disobedience, and the head of wretchedness. Then He, exalted is He, likened it to a tree described with three attributes:

The first attribute: it is corrupt. Some said it is garlic, because the Prophet (ﷺ) described garlic as a corrupt tree. [p. 96]
It was also said it is leek (al-kurrath). It was said it is the colocynth tree (al-hanzal), because of the many harms in it. It was said it is the thorn tree.

Know that this detailed specification is unnecessary, for a tree may be corrupt in terms of its smell, may be corrupt in terms of its taste, may be corrupt in terms of its form and appearance, and may be corrupt in terms of containing many harms. The tree that combines all these attributes, even if it does not exist, is nonetheless one whose attributes are known, so likening to it is beneficial for the intended goal.

The second attribute: His saying ﴿uprooted from the surface of the earth﴾. This attribute corresponds to His saying ﴿its root is firm﴾. The meaning of ijtuththat is "it was uprooted," and the real meaning of ijtithath is taking the whole body. His saying ﴿from the surface of the earth﴾ means that it has no root and no stem. Likewise, associating partners with God, exalted is He, has no proof, no stability, and no strength.

The third attribute: His saying ﴿having no stability﴾. This attribute is like a complement to the second attribute. The meaning is that it has no permanence. It is said: "The thing settled (qarra) a settling (qarar)," like your saying: "It remained firm, a firmness (thabat)." It likened to it the statement that is not supported by proof, which is therefore rejected and not established.

Know that this example describing the corrupt word is at the utmost perfection, because He, exalted is He, clarified that it is described as having many harms and is devoid of all benefits. As for it being described with harms, the reference to this is in His saying ﴿corrupt﴾, and as for it being devoid of all benefits, the reference to this is in His saying ﴿uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability﴾. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah makes firm those who believe with the firm word in the life of this world and in the Hereafter, and Allah leads astray the wrongdoers, and Allah does what He wills﴾.

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained that the attribute of the good word is that its root is firm, and the attribute of the evil word is that it has no firm root, but rather is cut off and has no stability, He mentioned that this firm word issuing from them in the life of this world necessitates the firmness of Allah's honour toward them and the firmness of His reward upon them. The purpose is to show that firmness in knowledge and obedience necessitates firmness in reward and honour from Allah, exalted is He. So His saying, ﴿Allah makes firm﴾, means: upon reward and honour. And His saying, ﴿with the firm word in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾, means: with the firm word that issued from them while they were in the life of this world.

Then He said: ﴿and Allah leads astray the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: just as the evil word has no firm root nor towering branch, so likewise the people of the evil word, who are the wrongdoers, Allah leads them astray from His honours and prevents them from succeeding in His reward.

There is another view concerning the verse, which is the well-known view: that this verse was revealed concerning the questioning of the two angels in the grave, and Allah's granting the believer the word of truth in the grave at the time of questioning, and His making him firm upon the truth. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said concerning His saying, ﴿with the firm word in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾, he said: "When he is asked in the grave: Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your Prophet? He says: My Lord is Allah, my religion is Islam, and my Prophet is Muhammad (ﷺ)."

As for the preposition "bi" in His saying, ﴿with the firm word﴾, the meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, only makes them firm in the grave because of their persistence in this saying during the life of this world. There is a rational argument for this statement: whenever persistence in an act is greater, the entrenchment of that state in the intellect and heart is stronger. Thus, whenever a servant's persistence in the remembrance of "there is no god but Allah" and in reflecting upon its realities and subtleties is more complete and perfect, the entrenchment of this knowledge in his intellect and heart after death will be stronger and more perfect.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: Whoever persists in the testimony during the life of this world, Allah makes him firm upon it in his grave and grants him its recitation.

He explained "the Hereafter" here as the grave, because the dead person, by death, is cut off from the rulings of this world and enters the rulings of the Hereafter.

His saying, ﴿and Allah leads astray the wrongdoers﴾, means: when the disbelievers are questioned in their graves, they say: "We do not know." And they only say that because Allah has led them astray.

His saying, ﴿and Allah does what He wills﴾, means: if He wills, He guides, and if He wills, He leads astray, and there is absolutely no objection to His action.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 14, verses 28–30:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favour of Allah for disbelief and caused their people to alight in the abode of ruin, into Hell, where they will burn, and what an evil place to settle?﴾ ﴿And they set up rivals to Allah, to lead [people] astray from His way. Say: "Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire."﴾

Know that Allah, the Exalted, returns in this verse to describing the states of the disbelievers. He says: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favour of Allah for disbelief?﴾ It was revealed concerning the people of Makkah, when Allah the Exalted settled them in His secure sanctuary and made their livelihood abundant, and sent Muhammad (ﷺ) among them, but they did not recognise the value of this favour. Then Allah the Exalted related of them several kinds of abominable deeds.

The first kind is His saying: ﴿exchanged the favour of Allah for disbelief﴾, and concerning it there are several interpretations:

First: It is possible that it means they exchanged the thanks (shukr) for the favour of Allah with disbelief, because when thanks became obligatory upon them on account of that favour, they responded with disbelief. It is as if they changed thanks into disbelief and substituted it.

Second: They exchanged the very favour of Allah for disbelief, because when they disbelieved, Allah took that favour away from them, so disbelief remained with them in place of the favour.

Third: Allah bestowed on them the Messenger and the Qur'an, but they chose disbelief over faith.

The second kind of what Allah related of them is His saying: ﴿and caused their people to alight in the abode of ruin﴾. Ruin (al-bawar) means destruction. It is said: "a man is bA'ir (ruined) and a people are bur (ruined)." From this is His saying: ﴿and you were a people of ruin﴾ [al-Fath: 12]. By "the abode of ruin" He means Hell, as evidenced by the fact that He explained it by Hell, saying: ﴿Hell, where they will burn, and what an evil place to settle﴾. Al-qarar means the place of settling, and it is a verbal noun that has been used as a name.

The third kind of their abominable deeds is His saying: ﴿And they set up rivals to Allah, to lead [people] astray from His way﴾, and concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: When Allah related of them that they exchanged the favour of Allah for disbelief, He mentioned that after they disbelieved in Allah, they set up rivals for Him. What is meant by this "setting up" is judgement, belief and speech. What is meant by "rivals" (andad) is likenesses and partners. This "partner" may have several meanings:

One of them: They assigned to the idols a share of what Allah had bestowed upon them, such as their saying: "This is for Allah, and this is for our partners."

The second: They associated the idols with the Creator of the worlds in worship.

The third: They used to openly affirm partners for Allah, such as their saying in the Hajj: "Here I am, O Lord, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours; You possess him and what he possesses."

Page 98

The second issue: Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *liyadilloo* (ليَضِلُّوا) with a fatha on the ya, from *dalla yadillu* (ضَلَّ يَضِلُّ). The rest read it with a damma on the ya, from *adalla ghayrahu yudillu* (أضَلَّ غَيْرَهُ يُضِلُّ), meaning "to lead another astray."

The third issue: The lam in His saying ﴿to lead [people] astray from His way﴾ is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), because worshipping idols is a cause that leads to misguidance. It may also be the lam of purpose (lam kay), meaning: those who took the idol so that they might lead others astray. This is when it is read with a damma, for then it may have the two meanings. But when it is read with a fatha, it can only be the lam of consequence, because they did not intend the misguidance of themselves. The explanation of the lam of consequence is that the purpose of a thing is not attained except at the last of its stages, as it is said: "The beginning of thought is the end of action." Whatever occurs as a consequence resembles the intended matter in this sense, and resemblance is one of the factors that justify the use of metaphor (majaz). For this reason, the lam is appropriately mentioned for consequence.

When Allah related of them these three kinds of abominable deeds, He said: ﴿Say: "Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire."﴾ The meaning is that the state of the disbeliever in this world, however it may be, is in comparison to the punishment he will reach in the Hereafter a matter of enjoyment and bounty. For this reason He said: ﴿Say: "Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire."﴾ Also, this address is to those concerning whom Allah related that they exchanged the favour of Allah for disbelief, and they were in the world amid many blessings. Therefore His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Say: "Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire."﴾ is fittingly used. This kind of imperative is called the imperative of threat (amr al-tahdid). Its parallel is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do whatever you wish﴾ [Fussilat: 40], and like His saying: ﴿Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire."﴾ [al-Zumar: 8].
