Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verse 31:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to My servants who have believed: establish prayer and spend from what We have provided for them, secretly and openly, before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, commanded the disbelievers, by way of threat and warning, to enjoy the bounties of this world, He commanded the believers in this verse to abandon enjoyment of this world and to strive hard with their souls and wealth. There are issues concerning this:

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "li-'ibadi" (My servants) with a sukun on the ya', while the rest read it with a fatha on the ya', because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn), so it was given a fatha for ease of pronunciation (naṣb).

The second issue: Regarding His saying ﴿yuqimu﴾ (let them establish) there are two possibilities:

The first: It may be a response (jawab) to an omitted command, which is the thing said. Its estimated form: "Say to My servants who have believed: Establish prayer and spend, and they will establish prayer and spend."

The second: It may be a command that was said, from which the lam of command has been omitted, meaning "li-yuqimu" (that they may establish), like your saying: "Say to Zayd: let him strike 'Amr." The lam was permitted to be omitted because His saying ﴿Say﴾ is a substitute for it. And if it were said at the outset, "yuqimu al-salah," it would not be permissible.

The third issue: After a person has completed faith, he has no power to dispose of anything except his own self or his wealth. As for the self, it must be occupied with serving the worshipped One in prayer; as for wealth, it must be expended in giving in obedience to Allah, exalted is He. These three are the recognised acts of obedience, namely faith, prayer and zakat. The full discussion of what must be said about these three matters we have mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3].

The fourth issue: The Mu'tazilah said: the verse indicates that provision is not unlawful, because the verse indicates that spending from provision is praiseworthy, and nothing spent from what is unlawful is praiseworthy, so it follows that provision is not unlawful. The explanation of this argument has passed many times.

The fifth issue: Regarding the grammatical status of His saying ﴿secretly and openly﴾ there are several possibilities:

One: that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning "possessors of secrecy and openness," i.e., those who give secretly and those who give openly.

Second: in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), meaning "at a time of secrecy and openness."

Third: in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "the spending of secrecy and the spending of openness," and the intended meaning is concealing voluntary charity and openly giving what is obligatory.

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, commanded the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat, He said: ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "bay'" here means ransom (fida'), and "khilal" means friendship (mukhallah), which is a verbal noun from khalaltu khilalan and mukhallatan, and it is friendship in companionship. Muqatil said: it is only a day in which there is no trade, no buying, no friendship and no kinship. It is as if Allah, exalted is He, is saying: spend your wealth in this world so that you may find the reward of that spending on a day like this, in which no transaction or friendship takes place. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿There is no trade in it, nor friendship, nor intercession﴾ [al-Baqarah: 254].

If it is said: How does He negate friendship in these two verses, when He affirmed it in His saying: ﴿The intimate friends that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67]?

We say: The verse which indicates the negation of friendship is to be understood as negating friendship arising from inclination of nature and desire of the soul, while the verse which indicates the affirmation of friendship is to be understood as the friendship that arises from servitude to Allah, exalted is He, and love for Allah, exalted is He. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: "It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth and sent down water from the sky, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. And He subjected for you the ships to sail through the sea by His command, and subjected for you the rivers. And He subjected for you the sun and the moon, constant in their courses, and subjected for you the night and the day. And He gave you of all that you asked of Him. And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, mankind is [often] a wrongdoer and ungrateful."

Know that when He had extended discourse on describing the conditions of the happy and the conditions of the wretched, and since the greatest foundation and the supreme station in attaining happiness is the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, through His essence and His attributes, while attaining wretchedness is the loss of this knowledge, He therefore concluded the description of the conditions of the happy and the wretched with the proofs indicating the existence of the Creator and the perfection of His knowledge and power.

Page 100

He mentions here ten kinds of proofs:

The first of them: the creation of the heavens.

The second: the creation of the earth, and to both of them refers His saying, exalted is He: "It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth."

The third: "And sent down water from the sky, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you."

The fourth: His saying: "And subjected for you the ships to sail through the sea by His command."

The fifth: His saying: "And subjected for you the rivers."

The sixth and seventh: His saying: "And subjected for you the sun and the moon, constant in their courses."

The eighth and ninth: His saying: "And subjected for you the night and the day."

The tenth: His saying: "And He gave you of all that you asked of Him." These ten proofs have been mentioned in this book, and their establishment and explanation have been given many times and in various ways. It is not amiss to mention here some benefits. Know that His saying, exalted is He, "Allah" is the subject (mubtada'), and His saying "who created" is its predicate (khabar). Then He, exalted is He, began by mentioning the creation of the heavens and the earth. We have mentioned in this book that the heavens and the earth indicate, in many respects, the existence of the Wise Creator. He began with mentioning them here because they are the two foundations upon which all the other proofs mentioned afterward branch out, for He said after them: "And sent down water from the sky, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you." And in this there are several discussions:

The first discussion: Without the sky, the sending down of water from it would not be possible, and without the earth, there would be nothing in which the water could settle. Thus it becomes clear that both must exist in order for this aim and this purpose to be achieved.

The second discussion: His saying, "And sent down water from the sky," and in this there are two opinions:

The first: that the water descended from the clouds, and the clouds were called "sky" (samā') derived from "sumuww," which means elevation.

The second: that He sent it down from the sky itself. This is far-fetched, because a person may be standing on the top of a high mountain and see the cloud below him; when he descends from that mountain, he sees that cloud raining upon them. And if this is a matter observed by sight, then disputing it is invalid.

Then, there is no doubt that each of the seven spirits divides into many branches, and each of those branches again into fine branches finer than a hair, and each of them has a passage to the organs. Moreover, those fine branches are very numerous, and each one has a particular wisdom. And it was said: a wrongdoer in hardship, he complains and panics; an ingrate in blessing, he hoards and withholds. What is meant by "the human being" here is the species; that is, the habit of this species is what we have mentioned. Here there are two investigations:

The first investigation: the human being is created with a disposition toward forgetfulness and boredom. Also, God's blessings are numerous, so whenever he tries to contemplate some of them, he becomes heedless of the rest.

The second investigation: He, exalted is He, said in this place: ﴿Indeed, the human being is surely a wrongdoer, a great ingrate﴾, and He said in Surah al-Nahl: ﴿Indeed, God is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 18]. When I reflected on this, a subtle point appeared to me: it is as if He says: when abundant blessings are obtained, you are the one who takes them and I am the one who gives them. The intended meaning is as if He says: if you are a wrongdoer, I am Most Forgiving; and if you are an ingrate, I am Most Merciful. I know your inability and your deficiency, so I do not respond to your shortcoming except with honour, and I do not repay your harshness except with fidelity. And we ask God for a good end and mercy.

The second investigation: He, exalted is He, said in this place: ﴿Indeed, the human being is surely a wrongdoer, a great ingrate﴾, and He said in Surah al-Nahl: ﴿Indeed, God is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 18]. When I reflected on this, a subtle point appeared to me: it is as if He says: when abundant blessings are obtained, you are the one who takes them and I am the one who gives them. So you acquire two attributes upon taking them: that you are a wrongdoer and a great ingrate; and I have two attributes upon giving them: that I am Most Forgiving and Most Merciful. The intended meaning is as if He says: if you are a wrongdoer, I am Most Forgiving; and if you are an ingrate, I am Most Merciful. I know your inability and your deficiency, so I do not respond to your shortcoming except with honour, and I do not repay your harshness except with fidelity. And we ask God for a good end and mercy.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: "It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth and sent down water from the sky, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. And He subjected for you the ships to sail through the sea by His command, and subjected for you the rivers. And He subjected for you the sun and the moon, constant in their courses, and subjected for you the night and the day. And He gave you of all that you asked of Him. And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, mankind is [often] a wrongdoer and ungrateful."

Know that when He had extended discourse on describing the conditions of the happy and the conditions of the wretched, and since the greatest foundation and the supreme station in attaining happiness is the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, through His essence and His attributes, while attaining wretchedness is the loss of this knowledge, He therefore concluded the description of the conditions of the happy and the wretched with the proofs indicating the existence of the Creator and the perfection of His knowledge and power.

Page 100

He mentions here ten kinds of proofs:

The first of them: the creation of the heavens.

The second: the creation of the earth, and to both of them refers His saying, exalted is He: "It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth."

The third: "And sent down water from the sky, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you."

The fourth: His saying: "And subjected for you the ships to sail through the sea by His command."

The fifth: His saying: "And subjected for you the rivers."

The sixth and seventh: His saying: "And subjected for you the sun and the moon, constant in their courses."

The eighth and ninth: His saying: "And subjected for you the night and the day."

The tenth: His saying: "And He gave you of all that you asked of Him." These ten proofs have been mentioned in this book, and their establishment and explanation have been given many times and in various ways. It is not amiss to mention here some benefits. Know that His saying, exalted is He, "Allah" is the subject (mubtada'), and His saying "who created" is its predicate (khabar). Then He, exalted is He, began by mentioning the creation of the heavens and the earth. We have mentioned in this book that the heavens and the earth indicate, in many respects, the existence of the Wise Creator. He began with mentioning them here because they are the two foundations upon which all the other proofs mentioned afterward branch out, for He said after them: "And sent down water from the sky, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you." And in this there are several discussions:

The first discussion: Without the sky, the sending down of water from it would not be possible, and without the earth, there would be nothing in which the water could settle. Thus it becomes clear that both must exist in order for this aim and this purpose to be achieved.

The second discussion: His saying, "And sent down water from the sky," and in this there are two opinions:

The first: that the water descended from the clouds, and the clouds were called "sky" (samā') derived from "sumuww," which means elevation.

The second: that He sent it down from the sky itself. This is far-fetched, because a person may be standing on the top of a high mountain and see the cloud below him; when he descends from that mountain, he sees that cloud raining upon them. And if this is a matter observed by sight, then disputing it is invalid.

The third discussion: Some people said that He brought forth these fruits by means of this water sent down from the sky according to the customary course; for in this meaning there is a benefit for the accountable, because when they know that these small benefits require that hardships and toils be endured in acquiring them, then the great and lasting benefits in the Hereafter are more deserving of enduring hardships in seeking them. And if a person forsakes rest and pleasures seeking these lowly goods, then it is more deserving that he forsake worldly pleasures in order to win the reward of Allah, exalted is He, and to be delivered from His punishment. For this reason, when the obligation ceases in the Hereafter, Allah, exalted is He, grants every soul what it desires without fatigue or toil. This is the view of the theologians (mutakallimun). Other people said: He, exalted is He, causes the fruits and crops to come into being by means of this water descending from the sky, and the matter is purely a theological one, and we have mentioned it in the chapter of al-Baqarah.

The fourth discussion: Abu Muslim said: The word "al-thamarat" (fruits) in most usage applies to what grows on trees, and it also applies to crops and plants, as in His saying: "Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit, and give its due on the day of its harvest" [al-An'am: 141].

* * *

The fifth discussion: He said, "and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you," and the meaning is that He, exalted is He, brought forth these fruits only so that they would be a provision for us, and the purpose is that He, exalted is He, intended by creating these fruits to convey goodness and benefit to the accountable; for kindness is not kindness unless the benefactor, by his act, intends to convey benefit to the one he benefits.

The sixth discussion: The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: His saying "min al-thamarat" (of the fruits) is an explanation of "rizqan" (provision), meaning: He brought forth thereby a provision which is fruits. It is also permissible that "min al-thamarat" be the object of "akhraja," and "rizqan" be a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the object, or an accusative of the verbal noun (masdar) of "akhraja," because it carries the meaning of "razaqa," and the sense is: "and He provided of the fruits a provision for you."

Page 101

As for the fourth proof, which is His saying: "And subjected for you the ships to sail through the sea by His command," and its parallel is His saying: "And among His signs are the ships in the sea like mountains" [al-Shura: 32]. In it there are discussions:

The first discussion: The benefit from what grows from the earth is only complete with the existence of ships running in the sea. This is because He, exalted is He, has assigned to each region of the earth a different kind of His bounties, so that when the bounty of one region is transported to the other side of the earth and vice versa, profit in trade increases. Moreover, this transport is not possible except by the ships of the land, which are camels, or by the ships of the sea, which are the ships mentioned in this verse. If it is said: What is the meaning of "And subjected for you the ships," given that the construction of a boat is one of the works of servants? We say: As for our position that the act of the servant is the creation of Allah, exalted is He, there is no question. As for the view of the Mu'tazilah, al-Qadi has answered it, saying: Were it not that He created the hard trees from which ships can be constructed, and were it not for His creating iron and the rest of the tools, and were it not for His teaching the servants how they may make them, and were it not that He created water with the property of flowing, by virtue of which the ship's sailing is valid, and were it not for His creating the winds and the strong motions in them, and were it not that He widened the rivers and made in them a depth that permits the sailing of ships, the benefit of ships would not have been realized. Thus, because He, exalted is He, is the Creator of these conditions, the Governor of these affairs, and the One who subjects them, it is proper to attribute the ships to Him.

The second discussion: He, exalted is He, attributed this subjection to His command, for a great king is rarely described as having "done" something; rather it is said of him that he "commanded" such-and-such, in glorification of his station. Some interpreted it according to the apparent meaning of His saying: "Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, 'Be,' and it is" [al-Nahl: 40]. The realization of this point returns to what we have mentioned.

The third discussion: The ship is one of the inanimate things, so its subjection is figurative, and the meaning is that since it runs upon the surface of the water as the sailor desires, it becomes as though it were an animal subjected to him.

The fifth proof: His saying, exalted is He: "And subjected for you the rivers." Know that the water of the sea is rarely used in agriculture; therefore, He, exalted is He, mentioned His bestowal upon creation by causing rivers and springs to gush forth, so that the water flows from them to the places of crops and plants. Also, the water of the sea is not fit for drinking, and the water suitable for this important purpose is the water of rivers.

The sixth and seventh proofs: His saying: "And subjected for you the sun and the moon, constant in their courses."

Know that the benefit of the sun and the moon is great, and Allah, exalted is He, has mentioned it in verses, among them His saying: "And made the moon therein a light and made the sun a lamp" [Nuh: 16]; among them His saying: "The sun and the moon [move] by calculation" [al-Rahman: 5]; among them His saying: "And placed therein a lamp and a luminous moon" [al-Furqan: 61]; and among them His saying: "It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light" [Yunus: 5].

As for His saying "dā'ibayn" (constant), the meaning of "du'ub" in the language is the passing of a thing in its work in a regular, continuous habit; it is said: "da'aba yad'abu da'aban wa du'ūban." We have mentioned this in His saying: "He said: You will sow for seven years in a continuous manner" [Yusuf: 47]. The exegetes said: His saying "dā'ibayn" means that they both continue in their motion, their illumination, and their effect in removing darkness and in the good order of plants and animals, for the sun is the sovereign of the day and the moon is the sovereign of the night. Were it not for the sun, the four seasons would not occur, and were it not for it, the interests of the world would be entirely disrupted. We have set out the benefits of the sun and the moon in detail at the beginning of this book.

Page 102

The eighth and ninth proofs: His saying: "And subjected for you the sun and the moon."

Know that their benefits are mentioned in the Qur'an, such as His saying, exalted is He: "And We made the night a covering, and We made the day for livelihood" [al-Naba': 10–11], and His saying: "It is He who made for you the night that you may rest therein, and the day giving sight" [Yunus: 67]. The theologians said: The subjection of the night and the day is figurative, because they are accidents (a'rad), and accidents are not subjected.

The tenth proof: His saying: "And He gave you of all that you asked of Him." Then, after He mentioned that great blessing, He explained that He did not limit Himself to it, but gave His servants of benefits and desires that cannot be enumerated or counted, so He said: "And He gave you of all that you asked of Him." The object is omitted, its estimated form being: "of every thing asked, a thing." It is also read "min kullin" with tanwin. "Mā sa'altumūhu" is a negation, and its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause, meaning: He gave you of all that, while you did not ask Him for it. It is also permissible that "mā" be a relative pronoun, and the estimate is: He gave you of all that what you needed and what your affairs and livelihoods could not be sound without; so it is as though you asked for it or sought it by the tongue of your state. Then, after mentioning these blessings, He concluded the discourse with His saying: "And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it." Al-Wahidi said: "Ni'mah" here is a noun put in the place of the verbal noun; it is said: "An'ama Allahu 'alayhi, yun'imu in'aman wa ni'mah," and the noun is put in place of the act of bestowing, as in His saying: "I spent on him infāqan and nafaqah," with the same meaning; therefore it is not made plural, because it has the sense of a verbal noun. The meaning of His saying "lā tuḥṣūhā" is that you are not able to enumerate all of them because of their abundance.

Know that when a person wishes to recognize that comprehending the categories of Allah's blessings is impossible, he should reflect upon a single thing so that he may know the incapacity of his own self regarding it, and we shall mention two examples of it.

The first example: physicians have mentioned that the nerves are of two kinds: some are cerebral (dimaghiyya) and some are spinal (nukhaiyya). As for the cerebral ones, they are seven. Then they have exhausted themselves in seeking to know the effects arising from each of those seven spirits. Then, there is no doubt that each of the seven spirits divides into many branches, and each of those branches again into fine branches finer than a hair, and each of them has a passage to the organs. If a single branch were to malfunction, whether because of its quantity, or its quality, or its position, the interests of the body would be disrupted. Moreover, those fine branches are very numerous, and each one has a particular wisdom. When a person reflects on this matter, he knows that God, exalted is He, has a great blessing upon the servant in accordance with each splinter of those nervous splinters, which, if lost, would greatly harm him, and he knows with certainty that he has no way to comprehend them or to be aware of their conditions. At this point he is certain of the truth of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you tried to count the favour of God, you could not number it﴾. Just as you have considered this in the nervous splinters, consider likewise the arteries and veins, and each of the simple and compound organs, in terms of quantity, quality, position, action and reception, until you see the divisions of this subject as an ocean without shore. And if you consider this in the body of one human being, then know the divisions of God's blessings in his soul and spirit, for the wonders of the world of spirits are greater than the wonders of the world of bodies. Then, when you have considered the state of a single animal, then consider the conditions of the world of the spheres and the stars, the layers of the elements, and the wonders of land and sea, plants and animals. At this point you will know that if the intellects of all creatures were combined and made into one intellect, and with that intellect a person contemplated the wonders of God's wisdom in the least of things, he would grasp only a little of them. Glorified is He, sanctified above the imaginations of those who imagine.

The second example: when you take a single morsel to place in your mouth, look at what came before it and what comes after it. As for the matters that came before it: know that this morsel of bread is not completed nor perfected unless this whole world stands upon the most correct form, because wheat is necessary, and it does not grow except with the help of the four seasons, the mixing of natures, and the appearance of winds and rains; none of these occurs except after the rotation of the spheres and the conjunction of some stars with others in specific manners of motion, and in their mode regarding direction, speed and slowness. Then, after the wheat is present, there must be tools for grinding and baking, and these do not come into being except when iron is generated in the wombs of mountains. Then, iron tools cannot be repaired except by other iron tools preceding them, and there must be an end to them in an iron tool which is the first of these tools. So consider how they came to be formed in these specific shapes. Then, when those tools have come into being, observe that there must be the gathering of the four elements, which are earth, water, air and fire, so that the bread can be baked from that flour. This is the consideration of what preceded the obtaining of this morsel.

As for the consideration of what comes after its obtaining: reflect on the composition of the animal's body, how God, exalted is He, created bodies such that they can benefit from that morsel, and how the animal is harmed by eating, and in which organs those harms occur. You cannot know the little of these things except by knowing the science of anatomy and the science of medicine in general. So it becomes clear from what we have mentioned that the benefit of a single morsel cannot be known except by knowing the totality of these matters, and the intellects are too limited to grasp an atom of these investigations. Thus, by this decisive proof, the truth of His saying, exalted is He, becomes clear: ﴿And if you tried to count the favour of God, you could not number it﴾. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the human being is surely a wrongdoer, a great ingrate﴾. It was said: he wrongs the blessing by neglecting its thanks, and is a great ingrate toward it. And it was said: a wrongdoer in hardship, he complains and panics; an ingrate in blessing, he hoards and withholds. What is meant by "the human being" here is the species; that is, the habit of this species is what we have mentioned. Here there are two investigations:

The first investigation: the human being is created with a disposition toward forgetfulness and boredom. When he finds a blessing, he forgets it immediately and wrongs it by failing to thank it; and if he does not forget it, he quickly becomes bored with it, and so falls into ingratitude for the blessing. Also, God's blessings are numerous, so whenever he tries to contemplate some of them, he becomes heedless of the rest.

The second investigation: He, exalted is He, said in this place: ﴿Indeed, the human being is surely a wrongdoer, a great ingrate﴾, and He said in Surah al-Nahl: ﴿Indeed, God is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 18]. When I reflected on this, a subtle point appeared to me: it is as if He says: when abundant blessings are obtained, you are the one who takes them and I am the one who gives them. So you acquire two attributes upon taking them: that you are a wrongdoer and a great ingrate; and I have two attributes upon giving them: that I am Most Forgiving and Most Merciful. The intended meaning is as if He says: if you are a wrongdoer, I am Most Forgiving; and if you are an ingrate, I am Most Merciful. I know your inability and your deficiency, so I do not respond to your shortcoming except with honour, and I do not repay your harshness except with fidelity. And we ask God for a good end and mercy.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verses 35–36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, make this city secure and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols."﴾ ﴿"My Lord, they have led many of the people astray. Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me — indeed, You are Forgiving and Merciful."﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, had made clear by the proofs mentioned earlier that there is no deity worthy of worship except God, glorified is He, and that it is absolutely impermissible to worship other than Him, He related about Abraham, peace be upon him, his exaggeration in denouncing the worship of idols.

Know also that God, exalted is He, related that Abraham, peace be upon him, asked God for several things:

The first of them is his saying: ﴿My Lord, make this city secure.﴾ The intended city is Mecca, and "secure" means possessing security.

If it is asked: What is the difference between his saying ﴿make this a secure city﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126] and his saying ﴿make this city secure﴾?

We say: In the first he asked that it be made among the cities whose inhabitants are safe and do not fear. In the second he asked that the quality it had, namely fear, be removed from it, and that its opposite, security, be established in it, as if he said: "It is a fearful city, so make it secure." Its explanation has already been given in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah.

* * *

The second: his saying: ﴿and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: It has been read as ﴿wa-jnubni﴾ (and keep me away), and there are three dialectal forms: janabahu, ajnabahu, and jannabahu. Al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz say janabani yajnubuni with the light form, while the people of Najd say jannabani sharrahu and ajnabani sharrahu. Its origin is placing a thing on the side and in a direction away from something else.

The second issue: One may say: the difficulty with this verse is from several aspects:

The first: Abraham, peace be upon him, asked his Lord to make Mecca secure, yet God did not accept his supplication, because a group destroyed the Ka'bah and raided Mecca.

The second: The prophets, peace be upon them, never worship idols at all, and if that is so, what is the benefit in his saying: "keep me away from worshipping idols"?

The third: He asked God not to make his sons among the worshippers of idols, yet God did not accept his supplication, because the disbelievers of Quraysh were among his descendants, even though they worshipped idols.

If they say: They were not the sons of Abraham but the sons of his sons, and the supplication is specific to the sons, we say: If by those sons is meant his sons from his loins, they were none other than Isma'il and Isaac, and both were among the great prophets, and it is known that prophets do not worship idols. So the question returns: what is the benefit of that supplication?

The answer to the first question has two aspects:

The first: It is related that when he finished building the Ka'bah, he made this supplication, and what is meant by it is making that land secure from ruin.

The second: What is meant is making its people secure, as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning the people of the town. This view is the one most exegetes adopt. On this interpretation, the answer is from two aspects:

The first aspect: the additional security that Mecca possesses, namely that whoever fearing takes refuge in Mecca becomes secure, and people, despite their intense enmity among themselves, meet in Mecca and do not fear one another. Among this is the security of wild animals, for they come close to people when they are in Mecca, while they are wary of people outside Mecca. This kind of security is present in Mecca, so the supplication must be understood in this sense.

The second aspect: What is meant by his saying ﴿make this city secure﴾ is the command and decree to make it secure, and that command and decree is certainly fulfilled.

As for the answer to the second question, al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "make me firm in avoiding their worship," as in His saying: ﴿and make us Muslims to You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128], meaning "make us firm in Islam."

One may say: The question remains, for since it is known that God makes the prophets, peace be upon them, firm in avoiding the worship of idols, what is the benefit of this request? In my view, the correct answer has two aspects:

The first: that although he, peace be upon him, knew that God would preserve him from worshipping idols, he mentioned that out of humbling himself and showing his need and dependence on God's grace in all requests.

The second: the Sufis say that shirk is of two kinds: overt shirk, which is what the polytheists hold, and hidden shirk, which is attaching the heart to intermediaries and apparent causes. Pure monotheism is that one's gaze is cut off from intermediaries and one sees no disposer except the Real, glorified and exalted is He. So it is possible that his saying ﴿keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ means that He preserve him from this hidden shirk, and God knows best what He intends.

As for the answer to the third question, there are several aspects:

The first: The author of al-Kashshaf said: His saying ﴿and my sons﴾ means his sons from his loins, and the benefit of this supplication is the very same benefit we mentioned in his saying ﴿keep me away﴾.

The second: Some said: he meant his children and the children of his children, every one of them who was alive at the time of the supplication, and there is no doubt that his supplication was answered regarding them.

The third: Mujahid said: none of Abraham's offspring worshipped an idol. An idol (sanam) is a sculpted image, and whatever is not sculpted is a wathan (idol-stone). The disbelievers of Quraysh did not worship sculpted images; they worshipped certain stones and certain trees. This answer is not strong, because it is not permissible for him, peace be upon him, to intend by this supplication anything other than the worship of other than God, and a stone is like an idol in that regard.

The fourth: This supplication is specific to the believing among his children, and the evidence for this is that he said at the end of the verse: ﴿Whoever follows me is of me﴾, which indicates that whoever does not follow him in his religion is not of him. A parallel to this is God's saying to Noah: ﴿He is not of your family; he is one whose conduct is unrighteous﴾ [Hud: 46].

The fifth: Perhaps, although he generalized in the supplication, God answered his supplication with regard to some and not others, and that does not entail belittling the prophets, peace be upon them. A parallel to this is God's saying concerning Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿He said, "Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people." He said, "And of my descendants?" He said, "My covenant does not include the wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124].

The third issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued from His saying ﴿and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ that disbelief and faith are from God, exalted is He. The argument is that Abraham, peace be upon him, asked God to keep him and his offspring away from disbelief, which shows that keeping away from disbelief and drawing near to faith is only from God, exalted is He. The Mu'tazilah's claim that it is to be understood as "lutf" (favours) is corrupt, because it is a departure from the apparent meaning, and because we have mentioned many aspects refuting that interpretation.

Then God, exalted is He, related about Abraham, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿My Lord, they have led many of the people astray.﴾ All sects agree that His saying ﴿they have led astray﴾ is figurative, because they are inanimate objects, and an inanimate object does not do anything at all; rather, since misguidance occurred during their worship, it was attributed to them, just as you say: "The world seduced them and deceived them," meaning they were seduced by it and deceived because of it.

Then he said: ﴿Whoever follows me is of me﴾, meaning whoever follows me in my religion and belief is of me, that is, is treated as part of me because of his special closeness to me and nearness to me. ﴿And whoever disobeys me in matters other than religion, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ Our companions argued from this verse that Abraham, peace be upon him, made this statement, and its purpose was intercession on behalf of the people of major sins among his community. The evidence for this is that his saying ﴿and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is explicit in asking forgiveness and mercy for those disobedient ones. So we say: those disobedient ones are either disbelievers or not. The first is false for two reasons:

The first: He, peace be upon him, made clear at the beginning of this verse that he is free of disbelievers, namely his saying ﴿keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾. Also, his saying ﴿whoever follows me is of me﴾ indicates by implication that whoever does not follow him in his religion is not of him and that he does not concern himself with setting right his affairs.

The second: The community is unanimous that intercession to remove the punishment of disbelief is not permissible. Since this has been refuted, it is established that his saying ﴿and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is intercession for disobedient ones who are not disbelievers.

Given this, we say: that disobedience is either among minor sins, or among major sins after repentance, or among major sins before repentance. The first and second are false, because his saying ﴿whoever disobeys me﴾ is unrestricted in its wording, so restricting it to minor sins is a departure from the apparent meaning. Moreover, minor and major sins after repentance are obligatory to be forgiven according to the opponents, so the wording cannot be applied to it. Thus it is established that this verse is intercession for removing punishment from people of major sins before repentance. And if this intercession is established on behalf of Abraham, peace be upon him, it is established on behalf of Muhammad ﷺ for several reasons:

The first: that no one distinguishes between them.

The second: that this rank is the highest of ranks, so if it were attained by Abraham, peace be upon him, while it is not attained by Muhammad ﷺ, that would be a deficiency in regard to Muhammad, peace be upon him.

The third: that Muhammad ﷺ is commanded to follow Abraham, peace be upon him, by His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90], and His saying: ﴿Then We revealed to you that you follow the religion of Abraham, a man of pure faith﴾. This is a close argument for establishing intercession for Muhammad ﷺ and for removing punishment from the people of major sins. And God knows best.

Having understood this, let us mention the statements of the exegetes. Al-Suddi said: its meaning is "whoever disobeys me and then repents." It was also said: this supplication was made before he knew that God does not forgive shirk. It was also said: "whoever disobeys me by persisting in disbelief, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful" means: You are able to forgive him and show mercy to him by transferring him from disbelief to Islam. It was also said: what is meant by this forgiveness is not to hasten punishment upon them but to give them respite until they repent, or that what is meant is not to hasten their death so that repentance escapes them. Know that these views are weak.

As for the first, namely restricting this intercession to disobedience on condition of repentance, we have already refuted it.

As for the second, namely the claim that this intercession was before he knew that God does not forgive shirk, we say: this is also far-fetched, because we have shown that the introduction of this verse indicates that Abraham's intention in this supplication cannot be intercession to remove the punishment of disbelief.

As for the third, namely the claim that what is meant by His being Forgiving and Merciful is that He transfer him from disbelief to faith, this too is far-fetched, because forgiveness and mercy imply the removal of punishment, and there is no indication in them of transfer from the attribute of disbelief to the attribute of faith. And God knows best.

As for the fourth, namely that forgiveness and mercy be understood as hastening punishment or leaving off hastening death, we say: this is false, because the disbelievers of our time are more numerous than them, and God has not hastened punishment or death upon them, although the people of Islam agree that they are neither forgiven nor shown mercy. So the interpretation of forgiveness and mercy as leaving off the hastening of punishment is refuted by this aspect. And what we have mentioned makes clear the soundness of what we have established as the argument. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verses 35–36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, make this city secure and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols."﴾ ﴿"My Lord, they have led many of the people astray. Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me — indeed, You are Forgiving and Merciful."﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, had made clear by the proofs mentioned earlier that there is no deity worthy of worship except God, glorified is He, and that it is absolutely impermissible to worship other than Him, He related about Abraham, peace be upon him, his exaggeration in denouncing the worship of idols.

Know also that God, exalted is He, related that Abraham, peace be upon him, asked God for several things:

The first of them is his saying: ﴿My Lord, make this city secure.﴾ The intended city is Mecca, and "secure" means possessing security.

If it is asked: What is the difference between his saying ﴿make this a secure city﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126] and his saying ﴿make this city secure﴾?

We say: In the first he asked that it be made among the cities whose inhabitants are safe and do not fear. In the second he asked that the quality it had, namely fear, be removed from it, and that its opposite, security, be established in it, as if he said: "It is a fearful city, so make it secure." Its explanation has already been given in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah.

* * *

The second: his saying: ﴿and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: It has been read as ﴿wa-jnubni﴾ (and keep me away), and there are three dialectal forms: janabahu, ajnabahu, and jannabahu. Al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz say janabani yajnubuni with the light form, while the people of Najd say jannabani sharrahu and ajnabani sharrahu. Its origin is placing a thing on the side and in a direction away from something else.

The second issue: One may say: the difficulty with this verse is from several aspects:

The first: Abraham, peace be upon him, asked his Lord to make Mecca secure, yet God did not accept his supplication, because a group destroyed the Ka'bah and raided Mecca.

The second: The prophets, peace be upon them, never worship idols at all, and if that is so, what is the benefit in his saying: "keep me away from worshipping idols"?

The third: He asked God not to make his sons among the worshippers of idols, yet God did not accept his supplication, because the disbelievers of Quraysh were among his descendants, even though they worshipped idols.

If they say: They were not the sons of Abraham but the sons of his sons, and the supplication is specific to the sons, we say: If by those sons is meant his sons from his loins, they were none other than Isma'il and Isaac, and both were among the great prophets, and it is known that prophets do not worship idols. So the question returns: what is the benefit of that supplication?

The answer to the first question has two aspects:

The first: It is related that when he finished building the Ka'bah, he made this supplication, and what is meant by it is making that land secure from ruin.

The second: What is meant is making its people secure, as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning the people of the town. This view is the one most exegetes adopt. On this interpretation, the answer is from two aspects:

The first aspect: the additional security that Mecca possesses, namely that whoever fearing takes refuge in Mecca becomes secure, and people, despite their intense enmity among themselves, meet in Mecca and do not fear one another. Among this is the security of wild animals, for they come close to people when they are in Mecca, while they are wary of people outside Mecca. This kind of security is present in Mecca, so the supplication must be understood in this sense.

The second aspect: What is meant by his saying ﴿make this city secure﴾ is the command and decree to make it secure, and that command and decree is certainly fulfilled.

As for the answer to the second question, al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "make me firm in avoiding their worship," as in His saying: ﴿and make us Muslims to You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128], meaning "make us firm in Islam."

One may say: The question remains, for since it is known that God makes the prophets, peace be upon them, firm in avoiding the worship of idols, what is the benefit of this request? In my view, the correct answer has two aspects:

The first: that although he, peace be upon him, knew that God would preserve him from worshipping idols, he mentioned that out of humbling himself and showing his need and dependence on God's grace in all requests.

The second: the Sufis say that shirk is of two kinds: overt shirk, which is what the polytheists hold, and hidden shirk, which is attaching the heart to intermediaries and apparent causes. Pure monotheism is that one's gaze is cut off from intermediaries and one sees no disposer except the Real, glorified and exalted is He. So it is possible that his saying ﴿keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ means that He preserve him from this hidden shirk, and God knows best what He intends.

As for the answer to the third question, there are several aspects:

The first: The author of al-Kashshaf said: His saying ﴿and my sons﴾ means his sons from his loins, and the benefit of this supplication is the very same benefit we mentioned in his saying ﴿keep me away﴾.

The second: Some said: he meant his children and the children of his children, every one of them who was alive at the time of the supplication, and there is no doubt that his supplication was answered regarding them.

The third: Mujahid said: none of Abraham's offspring worshipped an idol. An idol (sanam) is a sculpted image, and whatever is not sculpted is a wathan (idol-stone). The disbelievers of Quraysh did not worship sculpted images; they worshipped certain stones and certain trees. This answer is not strong, because it is not permissible for him, peace be upon him, to intend by this supplication anything other than the worship of other than God, and a stone is like an idol in that regard.

The fourth: This supplication is specific to the believing among his children, and the evidence for this is that he said at the end of the verse: ﴿Whoever follows me is of me﴾, which indicates that whoever does not follow him in his religion is not of him. A parallel to this is God's saying to Noah: ﴿He is not of your family; he is one whose conduct is unrighteous﴾ [Hud: 46].

The fifth: Perhaps, although he generalized in the supplication, God answered his supplication with regard to some and not others, and that does not entail belittling the prophets, peace be upon them. A parallel to this is God's saying concerning Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿He said, "Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people." He said, "And of my descendants?" He said, "My covenant does not include the wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124].

The third issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued from His saying ﴿and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ that disbelief and faith are from God, exalted is He. The argument is that Abraham, peace be upon him, asked God to keep him and his offspring away from disbelief, which shows that keeping away from disbelief and drawing near to faith is only from God, exalted is He. The Mu'tazilah's claim that it is to be understood as "lutf" (favours) is corrupt, because it is a departure from the apparent meaning, and because we have mentioned many aspects refuting that interpretation.

Then God, exalted is He, related about Abraham, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿My Lord, they have led many of the people astray.﴾ All sects agree that His saying ﴿they have led astray﴾ is figurative, because they are inanimate objects, and an inanimate object does not do anything at all; rather, since misguidance occurred during their worship, it was attributed to them, just as you say: "The world seduced them and deceived them," meaning they were seduced by it and deceived because of it.

Then he said: ﴿Whoever follows me is of me﴾, meaning whoever follows me in my religion and belief is of me, that is, is treated as part of me because of his special closeness to me and nearness to me. ﴿And whoever disobeys me in matters other than religion, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ Our companions argued from this verse that Abraham, peace be upon him, made this statement, and its purpose was intercession on behalf of the people of major sins among his community. The evidence for this is that his saying ﴿and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is explicit in asking forgiveness and mercy for those disobedient ones. So we say: those disobedient ones are either disbelievers or not. The first is false for two reasons:

The first: He, peace be upon him, made clear at the beginning of this verse that he is free of disbelievers, namely his saying ﴿keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾. Also, his saying ﴿whoever follows me is of me﴾ indicates by implication that whoever does not follow him in his religion is not of him and that he does not concern himself with setting right his affairs.

The second: The community is unanimous that intercession to remove the punishment of disbelief is not permissible. Since this has been refuted, it is established that his saying ﴿and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is intercession for disobedient ones who are not disbelievers.

Given this, we say: that disobedience is either among minor sins, or among major sins after repentance, or among major sins before repentance. The first and second are false, because his saying ﴿whoever disobeys me﴾ is unrestricted in its wording, so restricting it to minor sins is a departure from the apparent meaning. Moreover, minor and major sins after repentance are obligatory to be forgiven according to the opponents, so the wording cannot be applied to it. Thus it is established that this verse is intercession for removing punishment from people of major sins before repentance. And if this intercession is established on behalf of Abraham, peace be upon him, it is established on behalf of Muhammad ﷺ for several reasons:

The first: that no one distinguishes between them.

The second: that this rank is the highest of ranks, so if it were attained by Abraham, peace be upon him, while it is not attained by Muhammad ﷺ, that would be a deficiency in regard to Muhammad, peace be upon him.

The third: that Muhammad ﷺ is commanded to follow Abraham, peace be upon him, by His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90], and His saying: ﴿Then We revealed to you that you follow the religion of Abraham, a man of pure faith﴾. This is a close argument for establishing intercession for Muhammad ﷺ and for removing punishment from the people of major sins. And God knows best.

Having understood this, let us mention the statements of the exegetes. Al-Suddi said: its meaning is "whoever disobeys me and then repents." It was also said: this supplication was made before he knew that God does not forgive shirk. It was also said: "whoever disobeys me by persisting in disbelief, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful" means: You are able to forgive him and show mercy to him by transferring him from disbelief to Islam. It was also said: what is meant by this forgiveness is not to hasten punishment upon them but to give them respite until they repent, or that what is meant is not to hasten their death so that repentance escapes them. Know that these views are weak.

As for the first, namely restricting this intercession to disobedience on condition of repentance, we have already refuted it.

As for the second, namely the claim that this intercession was before he knew that God does not forgive shirk, we say: this is also far-fetched, because we have shown that the introduction of this verse indicates that Abraham's intention in this supplication cannot be intercession to remove the punishment of disbelief.

As for the third, namely the claim that what is meant by His being Forgiving and Merciful is that He transfer him from disbelief to faith, this too is far-fetched, because forgiveness and mercy imply the removal of punishment, and there is no indication in them of transfer from the attribute of disbelief to the attribute of faith. And God knows best.

As for the fourth, namely that forgiveness and mercy be understood as hastening punishment or leaving off hastening death, we say: this is false, because the disbelievers of our time are more numerous than them, and God has not hastened punishment or death upon them, although the people of Islam agree that they are neither forgiven nor shown mercy. So the interpretation of forgiveness and mercy as leaving off the hastening of punishment is refuted by this aspect. And what we have mentioned makes clear the soundness of what we have established as the argument. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verses 37–41 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation, by Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer. So make hearts among the people incline toward them, and provide for them from the fruits, that they may be grateful.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare, and nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven.﴾ ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq. Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication.﴾ ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and from my descendants. Our Lord, and accept my supplication.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day when the Reckoning takes place.﴾

Know that He, glorified and exalted, related about Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in this passage, that in his supplication he asked for seven matters.

The first requested matter: he asked Allah for the blessing of security, and this is his saying: ﴿My Lord, make this city secure﴾. Beginning with the request for the blessing of security in this supplication indicates that it is the greatest kind of blessing and goodness, and that nothing of the interests of religion and worldly life is complete without it. Some scholars were asked: "Is security better or health?" He said: "Security is better." The evidence for this is that if a sheep's leg is broken, it recovers after a time, and then it returns to grazing and eating; but if it is tied in a place and a wolf is tied near it, it refrains from fodder and does not touch it until it dies. This indicates that the harm arising from fear is greater than the harm arising from bodily pain.

The second requested matter: that Allah grant him monotheism and preserve him from polytheism, and this is his saying: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾.

The third requested matter: his saying: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation, by Your Sacred House﴾. His saying ﴿of my offspring﴾ means some of my offspring, namely Isma'il and those born of him. ﴿In a valley﴾ is the valley of Makkah. ﴿Without cultivation﴾ means that there is nothing of cultivation in it, like His saying: ﴿an Arabic Qur'an, without any crookedness﴾ [az-Zumar: 28], meaning there is no crookedness in it. ﴿By Your Sacred House﴾. They mentioned several reasons for calling it "the Sacred" (al-Muharram):

First: Allah forbade approaching it with disrespect or negligence, and made the area around it a sanctuary (haram) for its place.

Second: it has always been unassailable and mighty, which every tyrant reveres, like a forbidden thing that must be avoided.

Third: it was called "sacred" because it is respected and of great inviolability, and it is not permitted to violate it.

Fourth: it was forbidden to the Flood, meaning it was protected from it, just as it was called "ancient" (ʿatiq) because it was freed from it, so that no one could prevail over it.

Fifth: He commanded those who come to it to forbid themselves certain things that had been permitted to them before.

Sixth: He made the site of the House sacred when He created the heavens and the earth, and surrounded it with seven angels; it is like the House frequented (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur) which Adam built, and which was raised to the seventh heaven.

Seventh: He forbade His servants to approach it with blood, filth and other things. It is related that Hajar was a slave-girl of Sarah, who gave her to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and she bore him Isma'il, peace be upon him. Sarah said: "I was hoping that Allah would grant me a child from His friend, but He withheld it from me and granted it to my maidservant." She said to Ibrahim: "Remove the two of them from me." So he took them to Makkah while Isma'il was a suckling infant, then he returned. Hajar said: "To whom are you leaving us?" He said: "To Allah." Then he supplicated Allah, exalted, with his saying: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley﴾ to the end of the verse. Then she became thirsty and the child became thirsty, so she went with the child to the place of Zamzam, and he struck the ground with his foot and it gushed forth as a spring. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on the mother of Isma'il. Had she not hastened, Zamzam would have been a flowing spring." Then Ibrahim, peace be upon him, returned after Isma'il had grown up, and he, together with Isma'il, busied himself with raising the foundations of the House.

The judge (al-Qadi) said: Most of the matters mentioned in this narrative are remote, because it is not permissible for Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to transport his son to a place where there is no food or water, while he could have transported them to another town in the lands of al-Sham because of Sarah's words, unless we say that Allah informed him that water and food would be found there. I say: As for the appearance of the water of Zamzam, it may be a pre-miraculous sign (irhas) for Isma'il, peace be upon him, because that is permissible according to us, contrary to the Mu'tazilah; and according to the Mu'tazilah it is a miracle of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

Then he said: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled﴾. The lam is connected to "settled", meaning: I have settled a group of my offspring, namely Isma'il and his children, in this valley in which there is no cultivation, ﴿that they may establish prayer﴾.

Then he said: ﴿So make hearts among the people incline toward them﴾. Concerning this there are several discussions:

First discussion: al-Asma'i said: "Hawiya yahwa hawiyan (with fatha) means to fall from a height to a low place." It is also said: ﴿tahwi ilayhim﴾ means "desire them", and it is said: "hasten toward them". It is also said: "descend toward them and come down to them and alight." One says: "The stone fell (hawa) from the top of the mountain, yahwi, when it descended and poured down," and "the man fell (hawa) when he descended from the top of the mountain."

Second discussion: this supplication encompasses both religion and worldly life. As for religion, it includes the inclination of people to travel to that town for the sake of worship and obedience to Allah, exalted. As for worldly life, it includes the inclination of people to bring livelihoods to them through trade; because of this inclination their livelihood is widened, and their food and clothing abound.

Third discussion: the word "min" in His saying ﴿min an-nas (from the people)﴾ in ﴿So make hearts from the people incline toward them﴾ indicates partiality, and the meaning is: make the hearts of some of the people inclined toward them. Mujahid said: "If he had said 'the hearts of the people', Persia, the Romans, the Turks and the Indians would have thronged to it." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "If he had said 'the hearts of the people', the Jews, Christians and Magians would have performed pilgrimage, but he said: ﴿hearts from the people﴾, so they are the Muslims."

Then he said: ﴿and provide for them from the fruits﴾. Concerning this there are two discussions:

First discussion: he did not say "provide them with the fruits", but said ﴿provide for them from the fruits﴾, and this indicates that what is requested in the supplication is the delivery of some of the fruits to them.

Second discussion: it is possible that what is meant by delivering the fruits to them is delivering them to them by way of trade, and what is meant is the settling of villages near it in order to obtain fruits from them.

Then he said: ﴿that they may be grateful﴾. This indicates that the purpose for a sensible person of the benefits of this world is that he should devote himself to performing acts of worship and establishing acts of obedience, for Ibrahim, peace be upon him, made clear that he only asked for the facilitation of benefits for his children so that they might devote themselves to establishing the prayers and performing the obligations.

* * *

The fourth requested matter: his saying: ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare﴾.

Know that when he, peace be upon him, asked Allah to facilitate benefits for his children and make them easy for them, he mentioned that he does not know the outcomes of affairs and the ends of matters in the future, and that He, exalted, is the One who knows them and encompasses their secrets. So he said: ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare﴾. The meaning: You know better than us our conditions, our welfare and our corruptions. It is said: what we conceal is the grief arising from the separation between me and Isma'il, and what we declare is the weeping. It is also said: what we conceal is the sorrow firmly lodged in the heart, and what we declare refers to what passed between him and Hajar when she said to him at the parting: "To whom are you leaving us?" He said: "I leave you to Allah." She said: "Has Allah commanded you this?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Then we shall not fear."

Then he said: ﴿and nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

One: that it is the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, confirming Ibrahim, peace be upon him, like His saying: ﴿And thus they do﴾ [an-Naml: 34].

The second: that it is from the speech of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, meaning: nothing is hidden from Him who is the Knower of the unseen, of anything in any place, and the word "min" (of) indicates totality, as if it were said: nothing whatsoever is hidden from Him.

Then he said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾. Concerning this there are discussions:

First discussion: know that the Qur'an indicates that He, exalted, gave Ibrahim, peace be upon him, these two sons—I mean Isma'il and Ishaq—in old age and advanced years. As for the exact age, it is not known from the Qur'an, and it is referred to the narrations. It is said: when Isma'il was born, Ibrahim's age was ninety-nine years; when Ishaq was born, his age was one hundred and twelve years. It is also said: Isma'il was born to him when he was sixty-four years old, and Ishaq was born when he was ninety years old. And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: no child was born to Ibrahim until after he was one hundred and seventeen years old. He mentioned "in old age" because the favor of granting a child at this age is greater, in that this time is the time when despair of childbearing sets in, and attaining one's need at the time of despair is among the greatest blessings; and also because birth at that advanced age was a sign for Ibrahim.

If it is said: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, made this supplication when he settled Isma'il and his mother Hajar in that valley, and at that time Ishaq had not yet been born to him, so how could he say: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾?

We say: The judge (al-Qadi) said: this argument implies that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, uttered these words at another time, not directly after the preceding supplication. It is also possible to say that he, peace be upon him, made this supplication after Isma'il had grown up and Ishaq had appeared, although the apparent narrations contradict this.

Second discussion: the "ʿala" (in/upon) in His saying ﴿in old age﴾ means "with" (maʿa), as in the poet's saying:

"Indeed, despite what you see of my old age, I know where the shoulder is eaten (i.e., the best part)."

It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and its meaning is: He granted me in the state of old age.

Third discussion: concerning the connection between His saying ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare, and nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven﴾
[page 110]
and His saying ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾: it is as if there was in his heart a wish to ask Allah for their help and the help of their descendants after his death, but he did not state this request explicitly; rather he said: ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare﴾, i.e., You know what is in our hearts and our inner thoughts. Then he said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾, which apparently indicates that they will remain after his death, and that his heart is preoccupied with them; so this was a supplication for them for good and assistance after his death by way of allusion and indirect reference. This indicates that occupying oneself with praise at the time of need for supplication is superior to supplication itself. He, peace be upon him, said, relating from his Lord that He said: "Whoever is preoccupied with My remembrance rather than asking Me, I shall give him the best of what I give to those who ask." Then he said: ﴿Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾.

Know that when he mentioned the supplication by way of allusion and indirect reference, not by clear and explicit statement, he said: ﴿Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾, i.e., He knows the intended matter whether I state it explicitly or not. His saying "Hearer of supplication" is from the expression: "The king heard the words of so-and-so," when he takes them into account and accepts them; and from it: "Allah hears the one who praises Him."

* * *

The fifth requested matter: his saying: ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and from my descendants﴾. Concerning this there are issues:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verse 37–41 (part 2 of 2):

The first issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued from this verse that the actions of the servant are created by God, Exalted is He. They said: His saying, Exalted is He, quoting Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾, indicates that abstaining from what is forbidden only comes about from God. And His saying: ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and [also] from my descendants﴾ indicates that performing what is commanded only comes about from God. That is an explicit statement that Abraham, peace be upon him, was insistent that everything comes from God.

The second issue: The implied meaning of the verse, ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and [also] from my descendants﴾, is: and make some of my descendants so, because the word "min" (from/some of) in His saying ﴿and from my descendants﴾ is partitive (lit-tab'idh, indicating part). He mentioned this partitioning because he knew, by God's informing him, that there would be among his descendants a group of disbelievers, and that is His saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124].

The sixth matter: When he, peace be upon him, supplicated God regarding the aforementioned requests, he supplicated God, Exalted is He, that He accept his supplication, so he said: ﴿Our Lord, and accept my supplication﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means my worship, based on the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And I will withdraw from you and from what you invoke other than God﴾ [Maryam: 48].

* * *

The seventh matter: His saying: ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day when the reckoning is established﴾, and in it are two issues:

The first issue: One may say: seeking forgiveness only occurs after a prior sin, so this indicates that a sin had proceeded from him. Even though he was certain that God would forgive him, how could he ask for the attainment of what he was certain of attaining?

The answer: The purpose of it is to take refuge in God, Exalted is He, and to cut off all hope except in His bounty, generosity and mercy.

The second issue: If someone says: How was it permissible for him to seek forgiveness for his parents when they were both disbelievers?

The answer to this is in several respects:

First: The prohibition of it is only known through revelation (tawqif), so perhaps he had not found a prohibition on it and thus thought it was permissible.

Second: By "his parents" he meant Adam and Eve.

Third: That was on the condition of Islam.

And one may say: If the matter were so, that seeking forgiveness would not have been invalid; and if there were no such allowance, the saying of God, Exalted is He, would be void: ﴿except for the saying of Abraham to his father: "I will surely seek forgiveness for you"﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]. Some have said: his mother was a believer, and for this reason he singled out his father for mention in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of God, he disassociated himself from him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. And God knows best.

Regarding His saying: ﴿on the Day when the reckoning is established﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: "yaqum" means "yathbut" (is established, becomes firm), and it is used metaphorically from the standing of one who stands on his feet. The evidence for this is the saying: "the war stood on its shank" (qamat al-harb 'ala saqiha). A parallel is the saying "tarajjalat al-shams" (the sun rose on its feet), i.e., it shone and its light became firm, as if it had stood on one foot.

The second: That the standing of its people be attributed to the reckoning, by way of metonymy (majaz), like His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning its people. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verses 37–41 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation, by Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer. So make hearts among the people incline toward them, and provide for them from the fruits, that they may be grateful.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare, and nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven.﴾ ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq. Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication.﴾ ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and from my descendants. Our Lord, and accept my supplication.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day when the Reckoning takes place.﴾

Know that He, glorified and exalted, related about Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in this passage, that in his supplication he asked for seven matters.

The first requested matter: he asked Allah for the blessing of security, and this is his saying: ﴿My Lord, make this city secure﴾. Beginning with the request for the blessing of security in this supplication indicates that it is the greatest kind of blessing and goodness, and that nothing of the interests of religion and worldly life is complete without it. Some scholars were asked: "Is security better or health?" He said: "Security is better." The evidence for this is that if a sheep's leg is broken, it recovers after a time, and then it returns to grazing and eating; but if it is tied in a place and a wolf is tied near it, it refrains from fodder and does not touch it until it dies. This indicates that the harm arising from fear is greater than the harm arising from bodily pain.

The second requested matter: that Allah grant him monotheism and preserve him from polytheism, and this is his saying: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾.

The third requested matter: his saying: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation, by Your Sacred House﴾. His saying ﴿of my offspring﴾ means some of my offspring, namely Isma'il and those born of him. ﴿In a valley﴾ is the valley of Makkah. ﴿Without cultivation﴾ means that there is nothing of cultivation in it, like His saying: ﴿an Arabic Qur'an, without any crookedness﴾ [az-Zumar: 28], meaning there is no crookedness in it. ﴿By Your Sacred House﴾. They mentioned several reasons for calling it "the Sacred" (al-Muharram):

First: Allah forbade approaching it with disrespect or negligence, and made the area around it a sanctuary (haram) for its place.

Second: it has always been unassailable and mighty, which every tyrant reveres, like a forbidden thing that must be avoided.

Third: it was called "sacred" because it is respected and of great inviolability, and it is not permitted to violate it.

Fourth: it was forbidden to the Flood, meaning it was protected from it, just as it was called "ancient" (ʿatiq) because it was freed from it, so that no one could prevail over it.

Fifth: He commanded those who come to it to forbid themselves certain things that had been permitted to them before.

Sixth: He made the site of the House sacred when He created the heavens and the earth, and surrounded it with seven angels; it is like the House frequented (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur) which Adam built, and which was raised to the seventh heaven.

Seventh: He forbade His servants to approach it with blood, filth and other things. It is related that Hajar was a slave-girl of Sarah, who gave her to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and she bore him Isma'il, peace be upon him. Sarah said: "I was hoping that Allah would grant me a child from His friend, but He withheld it from me and granted it to my maidservant." She said to Ibrahim: "Remove the two of them from me." So he took them to Makkah while Isma'il was a suckling infant, then he returned. Hajar said: "To whom are you leaving us?" He said: "To Allah." Then he supplicated Allah, exalted, with his saying: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley﴾ to the end of the verse. Then she became thirsty and the child became thirsty, so she went with the child to the place of Zamzam, and he struck the ground with his foot and it gushed forth as a spring. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on the mother of Isma'il. Had she not hastened, Zamzam would have been a flowing spring." Then Ibrahim, peace be upon him, returned after Isma'il had grown up, and he, together with Isma'il, busied himself with raising the foundations of the House.

The judge (al-Qadi) said: Most of the matters mentioned in this narrative are remote, because it is not permissible for Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to transport his son to a place where there is no food or water, while he could have transported them to another town in the lands of al-Sham because of Sarah's words, unless we say that Allah informed him that water and food would be found there. I say: As for the appearance of the water of Zamzam, it may be a pre-miraculous sign (irhas) for Isma'il, peace be upon him, because that is permissible according to us, contrary to the Mu'tazilah; and according to the Mu'tazilah it is a miracle of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

Then he said: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled﴾. The lam is connected to "settled", meaning: I have settled a group of my offspring, namely Isma'il and his children, in this valley in which there is no cultivation, ﴿that they may establish prayer﴾.

Then he said: ﴿So make hearts among the people incline toward them﴾. Concerning this there are several discussions:

First discussion: al-Asma'i said: "Hawiya yahwa hawiyan (with fatha) means to fall from a height to a low place." It is also said: ﴿tahwi ilayhim﴾ means "desire them", and it is said: "hasten toward them". It is also said: "descend toward them and come down to them and alight." One says: "The stone fell (hawa) from the top of the mountain, yahwi, when it descended and poured down," and "the man fell (hawa) when he descended from the top of the mountain."

Second discussion: this supplication encompasses both religion and worldly life. As for religion, it includes the inclination of people to travel to that town for the sake of worship and obedience to Allah, exalted. As for worldly life, it includes the inclination of people to bring livelihoods to them through trade; because of this inclination their livelihood is widened, and their food and clothing abound.

Third discussion: the word "min" in His saying ﴿min an-nas (from the people)﴾ in ﴿So make hearts from the people incline toward them﴾ indicates partiality, and the meaning is: make the hearts of some of the people inclined toward them. Mujahid said: "If he had said 'the hearts of the people', Persia, the Romans, the Turks and the Indians would have thronged to it."
