Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "If he had said 'the hearts of the people', the Jews, Christians and Magians would have performed pilgrimage, but he said: ﴿hearts from the people﴾, so they are the Muslims."

Then he said: ﴿and provide for them from the fruits﴾. Concerning this there are two discussions:

First discussion: he did not say "provide them with the fruits", but said ﴿provide for them from the fruits﴾, and this indicates that what is requested in the supplication is the delivery of some of the fruits to them.

Second discussion: it is possible that what is meant by delivering the fruits to them is delivering them to them by way of trade, and what is meant is the settling of villages near it in order to obtain fruits from them.

Then he said: ﴿that they may be grateful﴾. This indicates that the purpose for a sensible person of the benefits of this world is that he should devote himself to performing acts of worship and establishing acts of obedience, for Ibrahim, peace be upon him, made clear that he only asked for the facilitation of benefits for his children so that they might devote themselves to establishing the prayers and performing the obligations.

* * *

The fourth requested matter: his saying: ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare﴾.

Know that when he, peace be upon him, asked Allah to facilitate benefits for his children and make them easy for them, he mentioned that he does not know the outcomes of affairs and the ends of matters in the future, and that He, exalted, is the One who knows them and encompasses their secrets. So he said: ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare﴾. The meaning: You know better than us our conditions, our welfare and our corruptions. It is said: what we conceal is the grief arising from the separation between me and Isma'il, and what we declare is the weeping. It is also said: what we conceal is the sorrow firmly lodged in the heart, and what we declare refers to what passed between him and Hajar when she said to him at the parting: "To whom are you leaving us?" He said: "I leave you to Allah." She said: "Has Allah commanded you this?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Then we shall not fear."

Then he said: ﴿and nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

One: that it is the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, confirming Ibrahim, peace be upon him, like His saying: ﴿And thus they do﴾ [an-Naml: 34].

The second: that it is from the speech of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, meaning: nothing is hidden from Him who is the Knower of the unseen, of anything in any place, and the word "min" (of) indicates totality, as if it were said: nothing whatsoever is hidden from Him.

Then he said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾. Concerning this there are discussions:

First discussion: know that the Qur'an indicates that He, exalted, gave Ibrahim, peace be upon him, these two sons—I mean Isma'il and Ishaq—in old age and advanced years. As for the exact age, it is not known from the Qur'an, and it is referred to the narrations. It is said: when Isma'il was born, Ibrahim's age was ninety-nine years; when Ishaq was born, his age was one hundred and twelve years. It is also said: Isma'il was born to him when he was sixty-four years old, and Ishaq was born when he was ninety years old. And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: no child was born to Ibrahim until after he was one hundred and seventeen years old. He mentioned "in old age" because the favor of granting a child at this age is greater, in that this time is the time when despair of childbearing sets in, and attaining one's need at the time of despair is among the greatest blessings; and also because birth at that advanced age was a sign for Ibrahim.

If it is said: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, made this supplication when he settled Isma'il and his mother Hajar in that valley, and at that time Ishaq had not yet been born to him, so how could he say: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾?

We say: The judge (al-Qadi) said: this argument implies that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, uttered these words at another time, not directly after the preceding supplication. It is also possible to say that he, peace be upon him, made this supplication after Isma'il had grown up and Ishaq had appeared, although the apparent narrations contradict this.

Second discussion: the "ʿala" (in/upon) in His saying ﴿in old age﴾ means "with" (maʿa), as in the poet's saying:

"Indeed, despite what you see of my old age, I know where the shoulder is eaten (i.e., the best part)."

It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and its meaning is: He granted me in the state of old age.

Third discussion: concerning the connection between His saying ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare, and nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven﴾
[page 110]
and His saying ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾: it is as if there was in his heart a wish to ask Allah for their help and the help of their descendants after his death, but he did not state this request explicitly; rather he said: ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare﴾, i.e., You know what is in our hearts and our inner thoughts. Then he said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾, which apparently indicates that they will remain after his death, and that his heart is preoccupied with them; so this was a supplication for them for good and assistance after his death by way of allusion and indirect reference. This indicates that occupying oneself with praise at the time of need for supplication is superior to supplication itself. He, peace be upon him, said, relating from his Lord that He said: "Whoever is preoccupied with My remembrance rather than asking Me, I shall give him the best of what I give to those who ask." Then he said: ﴿Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾.

Know that when he mentioned the supplication by way of allusion and indirect reference, not by clear and explicit statement, he said: ﴿Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾, i.e., He knows the intended matter whether I state it explicitly or not. His saying "Hearer of supplication" is from the expression: "The king heard the words of so-and-so," when he takes them into account and accepts them; and from it: "Allah hears the one who praises Him."

* * *

The fifth requested matter: his saying: ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and from my descendants﴾. Concerning this there are issues:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verse 37–41 (part 2 of 2):

The first issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued from this verse that the actions of the servant are created by God, Exalted is He. They said: His saying, Exalted is He, quoting Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾, indicates that abstaining from what is forbidden only comes about from God. And His saying: ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and [also] from my descendants﴾ indicates that performing what is commanded only comes about from God. That is an explicit statement that Abraham, peace be upon him, was insistent that everything comes from God.

The second issue: The implied meaning of the verse, ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and [also] from my descendants﴾, is: and make some of my descendants so, because the word "min" (from/some of) in His saying ﴿and from my descendants﴾ is partitive (lit-tab'idh, indicating part). He mentioned this partitioning because he knew, by God's informing him, that there would be among his descendants a group of disbelievers, and that is His saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124].

The sixth matter: When he, peace be upon him, supplicated God regarding the aforementioned requests, he supplicated God, Exalted is He, that He accept his supplication, so he said: ﴿Our Lord, and accept my supplication﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means my worship, based on the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And I will withdraw from you and from what you invoke other than God﴾ [Maryam: 48].

* * *

The seventh matter: His saying: ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day when the reckoning is established﴾, and in it are two issues:

The first issue: One may say: seeking forgiveness only occurs after a prior sin, so this indicates that a sin had proceeded from him. Even though he was certain that God would forgive him, how could he ask for the attainment of what he was certain of attaining?

The answer: The purpose of it is to take refuge in God, Exalted is He, and to cut off all hope except in His bounty, generosity and mercy.

The second issue: If someone says: How was it permissible for him to seek forgiveness for his parents when they were both disbelievers?

The answer to this is in several respects:

First: The prohibition of it is only known through revelation (tawqif), so perhaps he had not found a prohibition on it and thus thought it was permissible.

Second: By "his parents" he meant Adam and Eve.

Third: That was on the condition of Islam.

And one may say: If the matter were so, that seeking forgiveness would not have been invalid; and if there were no such allowance, the saying of God, Exalted is He, would be void: ﴿except for the saying of Abraham to his father: "I will surely seek forgiveness for you"﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]. Some have said: his mother was a believer, and for this reason he singled out his father for mention in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of God, he disassociated himself from him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. And God knows best.

Regarding His saying: ﴿on the Day when the reckoning is established﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: "yaqum" means "yathbut" (is established, becomes firm), and it is used metaphorically from the standing of one who stands on his feet. The evidence for this is the saying: "the war stood on its shank" (qamat al-harb 'ala saqiha). A parallel is the saying "tarajjalat al-shams" (the sun rose on its feet), i.e., it shone and its light became firm, as if it had stood on one foot.

The second: That the standing of its people be attributed to the reckoning, by way of metonymy (majaz), like His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning its people. And God knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation, by Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer. Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication.﴾ ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and from my descendants. Our Lord, and accept my supplication.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day when the Reckoning takes place.﴾

This indicates that the harm arising from fear is greater than the harm arising from bodily pain.

The second requested matter: that Allah grant him monotheism and preserve him from polytheism, and this is his saying: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾.

First: Allah forbade approaching it with disrespect or negligence, and made the area around it a sanctuary (haram) for its place.

Second: it has always been unassailable and mighty, which every tyrant reveres, like a forbidden thing that must be avoided.

Third: it was called "sacred" because it is respected and of great inviolability, and it is not permitted to violate it.

Fourth: it was forbidden to the Flood, meaning it was protected from it, just as it was called "ancient" (ʿatiq) because it was freed from it, so that no one could prevail over it.

Fifth: He commanded those who come to it to forbid themselves certain things that had been permitted to them before.

Sixth: He made the site of the House sacred when He created the heavens and the earth, and surrounded it with seven angels; it is like the House frequented (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur) which Adam built, and which was raised to the seventh heaven.

Seventh: He forbade His servants to approach it with blood, filth and other things. It is related that Hajar was a slave-girl of Sarah, who gave her to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and she bore him Isma'il, peace be upon him. Sarah said: "I was hoping that Allah would grant me a child from His friend, but He withheld it from me and granted it to my maidservant." She said to Ibrahim: "Remove the two of them from me." So he took them to Makkah while Isma'il was a suckling infant, then he returned. Hajar said: "To whom are you leaving us?" He said: "To Allah." Then he supplicated Allah, exalted, with his saying: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley﴾ to the end of the verse. One says: "The stone fell (hawa) from the top of the mountain, yahwi, when it descended and poured down," and "the man fell (hawa) when he descended from the top of the mountain."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "If he had said 'the hearts of the people', the Jews, Christians and Magians would have performed pilgrimage, but he said: ﴿hearts from the people﴾, so they are the Muslims."

Second discussion: it is possible that what is meant by delivering the fruits to them is delivering them to them by way of trade, and what is meant is the settling of villages near it in order to obtain fruits from them.

Then he said: ﴿that they may be grateful﴾. This indicates that the purpose for a sensible person of the benefits of this world is that he should devote himself to performing acts of worship and establishing acts of obedience, for Ibrahim, peace be upon him, made clear that he only asked for the facilitation of benefits for his children so that they might devote themselves to establishing the prayers and performing the obligations.

The fourth requested matter: his saying: ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare﴾.

It is said: what we conceal is the grief arising from the separation between me and Isma'il, and what we declare is the weeping. It is also said: what we conceal is the sorrow firmly lodged in the heart, and what we declare refers to what passed between him and Hajar when she said to him at the parting: "To whom are you leaving us?" He said: "I leave you to Allah." She said: "Has Allah commanded you this?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Then we shall not fear."

One: that it is the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, confirming Ibrahim, peace be upon him, like His saying: ﴿And thus they do﴾ [an-Naml: 34].

As for the exact age, it is not known from the Qur'an, and it is referred to the narrations. It is said: when Isma'il was born, Ibrahim's age was ninety-nine years; when Ishaq was born, his age was one hundred and twelve years. It is also said: Isma'il was born to him when he was sixty-four years old, and Ishaq was born when he was ninety years old. It is also possible to say that he, peace be upon him, made this supplication after Isma'il had grown up and Ishaq had appeared, although the apparent narrations contradict this.

Second discussion: the "ʿala" (in/upon) in His saying ﴿in old age﴾ means "with" (maʿa), as in the poet's saying:

"Indeed, despite what you see of my old age, I know where the shoulder is eaten (i.e., the best part)."

It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and its meaning is: He granted me in the state of old age.

and His saying ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾: it is as if there was in his heart a wish to ask Allah for their help and the help of their descendants after his death, but he did not state this request explicitly; rather he said: ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare﴾, i.e., You know what is in our hearts and our inner thoughts. The fourth requested matter: his saying: ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare﴾.

Know that when he, peace be upon him, asked Allah to facilitate benefits for his children and make them easy for them, he mentioned that he does not know the outcomes of affairs and the ends of matters in the future, and that He, exalted, is the One who knows them and encompasses their secrets. So he said: ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare﴾. The meaning: You know better than us our conditions, our welfare and our corruptions. It is said: what we conceal is the grief arising from the separation between me and Isma'il, and what we declare is the weeping. It is also said: what we conceal is the sorrow firmly lodged in the heart, and what we declare refers to what passed between him and Hajar when she said to him at the parting: "To whom are you leaving us?" He said: "I leave you to Allah." She said: "Has Allah commanded you this?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Then we shall not fear."

Then he said: ﴿and nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

One: that it is the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, confirming Ibrahim, peace be upon him, like His saying: ﴿And thus they do﴾ [an-Naml: 34].

The second: that it is from the speech of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, meaning: nothing is hidden from Him who is the Knower of the unseen, of anything in any place, and the word "min" (of) indicates totality, as if it were said: nothing whatsoever is hidden from Him.

Then he said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾. Concerning this there are discussions:

First discussion: know that the Qur'an indicates that He, exalted, gave Ibrahim, peace be upon him, these two sons—I mean Isma'il and Ishaq—in old age and advanced years. As for the exact age, it is not known from the Qur'an, and it is referred to the narrations. It is said: when Isma'il was born, Ibrahim's age was ninety-nine years; when Ishaq was born, his age was one hundred and twelve years. It is also said: Isma'il was born to him when he was sixty-four years old, and Ishaq was born when he was ninety years old. And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: no child was born to Ibrahim until after he was one hundred and seventeen years old. He mentioned "in old age" because the favor of granting a child at this age is greater, in that this time is the time when despair of childbearing sets in, and attaining one's need at the time of despair is among the greatest blessings; and also because birth at that advanced age was a sign for Ibrahim.

If it is said: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, made this supplication when he settled Isma'il and his mother Hajar in that valley, and at that time Ishaq had not yet been born to him, so how could he say: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾?

We say: The judge (al-Qadi) said: this argument implies that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, uttered these words at another time, not directly after the preceding supplication. It is also possible to say that he, peace be upon him, made this supplication after Isma'il had grown up and Ishaq had appeared, although the apparent narrations contradict this.

Second discussion: the "ʿala" (in/upon) in His saying ﴿in old age﴾ means "with" (maʿa), as in the poet's saying:

"Indeed, despite what you see of my old age, I know where the shoulder is eaten (i.e., the best part)."

It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and its meaning is: He granted me in the state of old age.

Third discussion: concerning the connection between His saying ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare, and nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven﴾
[page 110]
and His saying ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾: it is as if there was in his heart a wish to ask Allah for their help and the help of their descendants after his death, but he did not state this request explicitly; rather he said: ﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we declare﴾, i.e., You know what is in our hearts and our inner thoughts. Then he said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾, which apparently indicates that they will remain after his death, and that his heart is preoccupied with them; so this was a supplication for them for good and assistance after his death by way of allusion and indirect reference. This indicates that occupying oneself with praise at the time of need for supplication is superior to supplication itself. He, peace be upon him, said, relating from his Lord that He said: "Whoever is preoccupied with My remembrance rather than asking Me, I shall give him the best of what I give to those who ask." Then he said: ﴿Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾.

Know that when he mentioned the supplication by way of allusion and indirect reference, not by clear and explicit statement, he said: ﴿Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾, i.e., He knows the intended matter whether I state it explicitly or not. His saying "Hearer of supplication" is from the expression: "The king heard the words of so-and-so," when he takes them into account and accepts them; and from it: "Allah hears the one who praises Him."

* * *

The fifth requested matter: his saying: ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and from my descendants﴾. Concerning this there are issues:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verse 37–41 (part 2 of 2):

The first issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued from this verse that the actions of the servant are created by God, Exalted is He. They said: His saying, Exalted is He, quoting Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾, indicates that abstaining from what is forbidden only comes about from God. And His saying: ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and [also] from my descendants﴾ indicates that performing what is commanded only comes about from God. That is an explicit statement that Abraham, peace be upon him, was insistent that everything comes from God.

The second issue: The implied meaning of the verse, ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and [also] from my descendants﴾, is: and make some of my descendants so, because the word "min" (from/some of) in His saying ﴿and from my descendants﴾ is partitive (lit-tab'idh, indicating part). He mentioned this partitioning because he knew, by God's informing him, that there would be among his descendants a group of disbelievers, and that is His saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124].

The sixth matter: When he, peace be upon him, supplicated God regarding the aforementioned requests, he supplicated God, Exalted is He, that He accept his supplication, so he said: ﴿Our Lord, and accept my supplication﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means my worship, based on the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And I will withdraw from you and from what you invoke other than God﴾ [Maryam: 48].

* * *

The seventh matter: His saying: ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day when the reckoning is established﴾, and in it are two issues:

The first issue: One may say: seeking forgiveness only occurs after a prior sin, so this indicates that a sin had proceeded from him. Even though he was certain that God would forgive him, how could he ask for the attainment of what he was certain of attaining?

The answer: The purpose of it is to take refuge in God, Exalted is He, and to cut off all hope except in His bounty, generosity and mercy.

The second issue: If someone says: How was it permissible for him to seek forgiveness for his parents when they were both disbelievers?

The answer to this is in several respects:

First: The prohibition of it is only known through revelation (tawqif), so perhaps he had not found a prohibition on it and thus thought it was permissible.

Second: By "his parents" he meant Adam and Eve.

Third: That was on the condition of Islam.

And one may say: If the matter were so, that seeking forgiveness would not have been invalid; and if there were no such allowance, the saying of God, Exalted is He, would be void: ﴿except for the saying of Abraham to his father: "I will surely seek forgiveness for you"﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]. Some have said: his mother was a believer, and for this reason he singled out his father for mention in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of God, he disassociated himself from him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. And God knows best.

Regarding His saying: ﴿on the Day when the reckoning is established﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: "yaqum" means "yathbut" (is established, becomes firm), and it is used metaphorically from the standing of one who stands on his feet. The evidence for this is the saying: "the war stood on its shank" (qamat al-harb 'ala saqiha). A parallel is the saying "tarajjalat al-shams" (the sun rose on its feet), i.e., it shone and its light became firm, as if it had stood on one foot.

The second: That the standing of its people be attributed to the reckoning, by way of metonymy (majaz), like His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning its people. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 14, verses 42–43:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only defers them to a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾ ﴿hastening forward, with heads raised, their glance not returning to them, and their hearts empty.﴾

Know that when He had shown the proofs of monotheism (tawhid), and then related that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, asked Allah to preserve him from associating partners with Him, asked Him to enable him to do righteous deeds, and asked that He single him out with mercy and forgiveness on the Day of Resurrection, He then mentioned what indicates the existence of the Day of Resurrection and what indicates its attributes. As for what indicates the existence of the Resurrection, it is His saying: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do.﴾ The purpose of this is to draw attention to the fact that if He, Exalted is He, did not avenge the oppressed against the oppressor, it would follow that He is either unaware of that oppressor, or unable to take revenge, or content with that injustice. Since unawareness, incapacity, and contentment with injustice are impossible for Allah, it is impossible that He would not take revenge on the oppressor on behalf of the oppressed.

If it is said: How is it fitting for the Messenger (ﷺ) to think that Allah is described by unawareness?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: What is meant is to affirm him in what he already was, namely that he does not think Allah is unaware, like His saying: ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 14], ﴿And do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ [al-Qasas: 88], and like His saying: ﴿O you who believe.﴾

The second: The purpose is to explain that if He did not take revenge, the non-retaliation would be due to His unawareness of that injustice. Since the impossibility of this unawareness is known to everyone, it is necessarily the case that non-retaliation is impossible.

The third: What is meant is: do not think that He deals with them as one who is unaware of what they do, but rather as a watcher over them who calls them to account for the smallest and the least.

The fourth: Although this speech is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) outwardly, in reality it is addressed to the community. It is related from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna that it is a consolation for the oppressed and a threat to the oppressor. Then Allah, Exalted is He, explained that He only defers the punishment of these wrongdoers to a Day described by attributes.

The first attribute: ﴿when eyes will stare fixedly.﴾ It is said: the gaze of a man became fixed (shakhasa) when his eye remains open without blinking. The fixed staring of the eye indicates bewilderment, astonishment, and the loss of strength.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿hastening forward (muhti'in)﴾. There are four opinions on the meaning of ihta':

The first opinion: Abu 'Ubayda said it means hurrying. It is said: the camel hastened (ahta'a) in its walking, and stahta'a when it hurried. According to this meaning, the sense is: the usual state of one whose gaze remains fixed out of intense fear is that he remains standing still. So Allah, Exalted is He, explained that their state is contrary to this usual condition: despite their eyes being fixed, they are hastening (muhti'in), that is, rushing toward that affliction.

The second opinion on ihta': Ahmad ibn Yahya said: the muhti' is one who looks in humiliation and submissiveness.

The third opinion: the muhti' is one who is silent.

The fourth opinion: al-Layth said: it is said of a man when he is still and humbled: ahta'a.

The third attribute: His saying: ﴿with heads raised (muqni'i ru'usihim)﴾. Iqna' is raising the head while looking in humiliation and submissiveness. So His saying muqni'i ru'usihim means raising their heads. The meaning is that the usual behavior of one who witnesses an affliction is to lower his head so that he does not see it. So Allah, Exalted is He, explained that their state is contrary to this usual behavior, and that they raise their heads.

The fourth attribute: His saying: ﴿their glance not returning to them.﴾ What is meant by this attribute is the continuation of that fixed staring. His saying ﴿when eyes will stare fixedly﴾ [Ibrahim: 42] does not indicate that this staring is constant, but His saying ﴿their glance not returning to them﴾ indicates the continuation of this staring, and that indicates the continuation of that bewilderment and astonishment in their hearts.

The fifth attribute: His saying: ﴿and their hearts empty (hawa')﴾. Hawa' is an empty void not occupied by bodies, and then it was used as a description, so it is said: "the heart of so-and-so is hawa'" when it is empty and has no strength in it. The purpose is to explain that the hearts of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection are empty of all thoughts and reflections because of the magnitude of the bewilderment that befalls them, and of every hope and expectation because of what they have realized of the punishment, and of every joy because of the abundance of grief within them.

Having known these five attributes, they differed about the time of their occurrence. It was said: they occur at the reckoning, based on the evidence that He mentioned these attributes right after describing that Day as the Day when the reckoning will be established. It was also said: they occur when the people are separated into groups, the blessed going to Paradise and the wretched to Hell. And it was said: rather, they occur when the summoner calls and people rise from the graves. The first is preferable because of the evidence we have mentioned. And Allah knows best.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 14, verses 44–45:

God Most High says: ﴿And warn the people of the day when the punishment comes to them, and those who did wrong will say, "Our Lord, delay us for a short term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers." Had you not sworn before, "You will have no cessation"?﴾ ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, and it became clear to you how We dealt with them, and We set forth the parables for you.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿the day when the punishment comes to them﴾ contains several discussions:

The first discussion: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: ﴿the day when the punishment comes to them﴾ is the second object of ﴿warn﴾, and it is the Day of Resurrection.

The second discussion: The alif and lam in the word ﴿the punishment﴾ refer to a previously known thing. That is: "And warn the people of the day when there comes to them the punishment that was mentioned before, which is the fixing of their gaze and their being hurried, with their heads raised."

The third discussion: Warning (indhar) is frightening by mentioning harms. The exegetes are agreed that His saying ﴿the day when the punishment comes to them﴾ is the Day of Resurrection. Abu Muslim interpreted it as the time of direct witnessing (of the punishment). The apparent sense of the text contradicts this, because God Most High describes the day, saying that their punishment comes in it, and that they ask for a return, and it is said to them: ﴿Had you not sworn before, "You will have no cessation"?﴾, and this is fitting only for the Day of Resurrection. The argument of Abu Muslim is that this verse resembles His saying: ﴿And spend of what We have provided you before death comes to one of you, and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me to a near term so that I could give charity and be among the righteous."﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10]. Then God, glorified is He, related what the disbelievers say on that day, saying: ﴿Those who wronged will say, "Our Lord, delay us for a short term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers."﴾

The exegetes differed about the meaning of His saying ﴿delay us for a short term﴾. Some of them said: they sought a return to the world so that they might make up for what they neglected. Others said: rather, they sought a return to the state of obligation (taklif), by the evidence of their saying: ﴿we will answer Your call and follow the messengers.﴾

As for the view of Abu Muslim, the interpretation of this verse is clear. God Most High says, answering them: ﴿Had you not sworn before, "You will have no cessation"?﴾ Its meaning is what God Most High mentioned in another verse, namely His saying: ﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that God will not raise up those who die﴾ [al-Nahl: 38], and other such things that they used to say in denying the Return. God Most High rebuked them with this statement, because rebuke with this kind of thing is stronger. As for the meaning of ﴿You will have no cessation﴾, there is no doubt that they used to say: "We will have no cessation from this life to another life, and from this abode to the abode of recompense." They did not deny that they would pass from life to death, or from youth to old age, or from poverty to wealth. Then God Most High added another rebuke by His saying: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾, meaning: you dwelt in the dwellings of those who disbelieved before you, namely the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud, who wronged themselves through disbelief and disobedience. For whoever witnesses these conditions is obliged to take warning, and if he does not take warning, he deserves blame and rebuke.

Then He said: ﴿and it became clear to you how We dealt with them﴾, and it became apparent to you that their end led to ruin, disgrace and punishment.

If it is asked: Why was it said ﴿and it became clear to you how We dealt with them﴾, when the people did not acknowledge that God destroyed them because of their denial?

We answer: They knew that those earlier people were seeking the world, then they perished and were wiped out. At this point they know that there is no benefit in seeking the world, and that what is obligatory is earnestness and striving in seeking the religion. Whoever recognizes this must be fearful and anxious, and this becomes a deterrent for him. This is when it is read with the letter ta' (tubayyana). As for when it is read with the letter nun (nubayyin), there is no doubt about it, because the sense is as if He, Exalted, had said: "Did We not make clear to you how We dealt with them?" and not everything that was made clear to them was understood by them.

As for His saying ﴿and We set forth the parables for you﴾, what is meant is what God revealed in the Qur'an by which it is known that He is capable of the resurrection as He was capable of the first creation, and capable of deferred punishment as He carries out immediate destruction. And that is abundant in the Book of God. And God knows best.
